articles.title: US Brings $12 Billion to Uzbekistan—Russia Brings Tanks and Troops - UNITED24 Media
articles.summary: US Brings $12 Billion to Uzbekistan—Russia Brings Tanks and Troops  UNITED24 Media
articles.full_text:
Uzbekistan has signed $12 billion worth of agreements with American companies while welcoming Russian troops for joint military exercises near its border with Afghanistan, highlighting the Central Asian country’s growing economic ties with Washington alongside its continued defense cooperation with Moscow.
According to Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade, 54 agreements with US companies were signed in Samarkand on October 19. Just one day later, Russian and Uzbek forces launched the Hamkorlik-2026 military exercises at the Termez training ground in southern Uzbekistan, according to Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Defense.
The American agreements cover critical minerals, energy, transportation, financial services, digital technologies, and industrial development. Companies involved include GE Aerospace, Wabtec, BlackRock, Citigroup, and Franklin Templeton.
The $12 billion figure represents the announced value of the agreements rather than funds already invested.
The deals come as Washington seeks to expand its economic influence in Central Asia, a region where Russia and China have traditionally maintained strong political, economic, and security ties.
Russian troops from the 201st Military Base in neighboring Tajikistan traveled more than 300 kilometers through mountainous terrain to reach the training ground near the Afghan border.
The Russian military column included BTR-82A armored personnel carriers, Ural military trucks, and specialized vehicles based on KamAZ chassis.
The exercises focus on detecting and eliminating simulated armed groups operating in border areas. Russian and Uzbek forces are expected to deploy reconnaissance and attack drones, ground robotic systems, mountain assault units, and Mi-24 attack helicopters.
The military cooperation reflects an established relationship between Moscow and Tashkent. The two countries conducted similar exercises at the same training ground in July 2025 and have agreed on a defense cooperation plan covering 2026–2030.
Earlier in October, Russia conducted the Center-2026 military exercises involving more than 47,000 troops, during which its forces rehearsed an offensive into a neighboring Central Asian country and the establishment of a “security zone” on its territory. Although Moscow did not identify the country, the location of the drills suggested Kazakhstan as the potential target.

articles.title: ‘Freeze and Stop!’ Zelensky Tells Fox News’ Brian Kilmeade He Would ‘Accept’ End of War Along Current Frontlines - Mediaite
articles.summary: ‘Freeze and Stop!’ Zelensky Tells Fox News’ Brian Kilmeade He Would ‘Accept’ End of War Along Current Frontlines  Mediaite
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Wednesday he would accept freezing the war along its current frontlines, publicly embracing a ceasefire framework that would leave Russia in control of territory it presently occupies while negotiations continue.
Appearing on Fox & Friends, Zelensky was pressed by co-host Brian Kilmeade on whether he would accept an agreement that effectively stopped the fighting where the battlefield stands today.
“Would you accept a peace deal that freezes everything the way it is right now, where you still keep 75% or more of your country?” Kilmeade asked.
“Yes,” Zelensky replied. “Right now, we have to freeze and I think this is [the] real way to end this war.”
He added: “We call it ceasefire or ‘stop killing’ as President Trump called it. Freeze and stop.”
Zelensky stressed that such a halt would be only the first step, arguing that any deal would need firm guarantees to prevent Russia from restarting the war: “And, of course, this is [the] minimum [of] what we need from Russia today. Then we will go to the president and Europeans and ask [for] security guarantees.”
“The most important is peace and also security [of] peace,” Zelensky continued. “Not to be afraid that occupation will come back, aggression will come back, killings will come back. We have to stop this and that’s why [we need] freeze and talks. And security guarantees from the United States and prosperity from our partners for innovation of our lives.”
His remarks come as President Donald Trump intensifies pressure on Kyiv to reach a settlement with Moscow. Trump has repeatedly promoted the idea of stopping the fighting along the existing front, while Russia has continued to demand control over additional Ukrainian territory, including areas of Donetsk that its forces do not currently occupy.
The two sides remain far apart on the final status of occupied territory and the shape of any postwar security arrangement. Moscow has also continued to oppose Ukrainian NATO membership, while Kyiv has pressed Washington and European governments for binding guarantees against renewed Russian aggression.
Zelensky framed a frontline “freeze” as a way to move from combat into negotiations rather than a final territorial settlement, and help rebuilding Ukraine.
“We need 9.5 million people which are broad everywhere,” Zelensky said. “We need them to come back to Ukraine, just to live and to build their country.”

articles.title: Georgia appoints special representative for relations with Russia after post was vacant for almost a year - OC Media
articles.summary: Georgia appoints special representative for relations with Russia after post was vacant for almost a year  OC Media
articles.full_text:
Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze has appointed Giorgi Zurabashvili as his special representative for relations with Russia, a post that has been vacant since December 2025.
Georgia and Russia have had no diplomatic relations since the 2008 war, which ended with Russia recognising the independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, two breakaway regions internationally recognised as part of Georgia. Despite the absence of diplomatic ties, Russia and Georgia maintain trade and economic relations, while the Geneva International Discussions and the special representative’s position provide channels for dialogue.
Kobakhidze announced the appointment on Wednesday, describing the role as important for maintaining dialogue with Moscow amid the absence of diplomatic relations between Georgia and Russia.
‘The peaceful resolution of the conflict with the Russian Federation, the preservation and development of existing trade and economic relations, and maintaining ongoing dialogue on humanitarian issues are among our country’s most important priorities’, Kobakhidze said.
He added that, alongside the Geneva International Discussions, the prime minister’s special representative played a key role in pursuing these objectives.
Kobakhidze described Zurabashvili as an experienced diplomat who had held several senior public service positions over the years, including directorships at various departments of the Foreign Ministry and an ambassadorship.
Zurabashvili was appointed Deputy Foreign Minister in 2024 and First Deputy Foreign Minister on 1 July 2025.
‘We are confident that Giorgi Zurabashvili will use his knowledge and experience to fulfil the responsibilities entrusted to him as the Prime Minister’s special representative’, Kobakhidze added.
In response to a journalist’s question, Kobakhidze stated that the appointment did not signal a new stage in Georgia’s relations with Russia.
Zurabashvili will retain his position at the Foreign Ministry. However, Kobakhidze said that he would represent Georgia in relations with Russia in his capacity as the Prime Minister’s special representative.
‘I will do everything in my power to fulfil the tasks that Georgia needs me to carry out’, Zurabashvili said.
The position of the Prime Minister’s special representative for relations with Russia became vacant in December 2025, when Giorgi Kajaja left the post.
Before Kajaja, Zurab Abashidze held the position for 12 years, from 2012 to 2024, serving as the prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia, in the so-called Abashidze–Karasin format, a bilateral dialogue mechanism between Georgia and Russia.
On 6 October, the Foreign Ministry announced that Abashidze had been appointed Georgia’s non-resident ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary to Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, and Albania.
For ease of reading, we choose not to use qualifiers such as ‘de facto’, ‘unrecognised’, or ‘partially recognised’ when discussing institutions or political positions within Abkhazia, Nagorno-Karabakh, and South Ossetia. This does not imply a position on their status.

articles.title: Kazakhstan’s proposal: How C5+ with the US strengthened Central Asia’s global role - Qazinform
articles.summary: Kazakhstan’s proposal: How C5+ with the US strengthened Central Asia’s global role  Qazinform
articles.full_text:
The evolution of the C5+1 format, its key achievements in strengthening cooperation between Central Asia and the United States, and its future prospects amid global geopolitical challenges were among the key topics discussed by Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations Kairat Umarov in an exclusive interview with Silk Way TV Channel, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
- The C5+ format has become an important mechanism for strengthening Central Asia’s cooperation with global partners. Kazakhstan played an initiating role in advancing this format as early as 2013. Could you tell us how the idea emerged and evolved into the diplomatic platform we see today?
- This is a very interesting question because, as you said, I was personally involved in the creation of the C5+ format. Even before C5+1 with the United States began, similar platforms already existed, such as Central Asia+Japan, Central Asia+South Korea, and Central Asia+European Union.
When the idea of creating a similar format with the United States emerged, we started discussing it with the State Department.
At that time, the idea was not so popular in the United States because they traditionally discussed Central Asian affairs with countries like Russia and China. The idea was to find a different way for the United States to talk directly to Central Asian ministers, without going through other countries.
Of course, this was not exclusive, and they could continue the same consultations with those countries, but it was very important to have those direct discussions and contacts with Central Asian countries. The idea was born even earlier than 2013.
It was my good friend, whom I had known for many years, Dr. Frederick Starr, who is the chairman of the Central Asia-Caucasus Institute at Johns Hopkins. He was extensively working on Central Asia and the wider region. He knows quite a bit about the history and developments.
When I was appointed ambassador to Washington in 2013 and arrived in January in Washington, D.C., I had to meet with some of my friends from previous engagements. One of the first meetings was with Frederick Starr, and he told me that he had proposed such an idea in his book: a mechanism for the US Secretary of State to meet with the foreign ministers of Central Asia. Maybe it was not exactly the same, but he was talking about this kind of interaction, and he said that nobody paid attention to it.
The idea was very topical and useful, but the US administration was not taking it forward. I said to him, "Okay, let's work together on this issue," and I proposed it to the State Department. At that time, there was a change in leadership. It was the second term of President Obama, and there was new leadership in Central Asian and South Asian affairs. Nisha Biswal became the Assistant Secretary of State, and we talked about this idea. She said, "Okay, let's look at that, but no promises." Two years later, she came back to me and said that the idea had received...
- It took two years to decide.
- It took them 2 years, I think, to consult with those who were somehow engaged in the field, so to say, at the State Department and maybe some other structures.
But the idea was to have this direct contact with Central Asian countries, and she came up with this idea. Instead of Central Asia plus US, she said, why don't we just make a shortened version, C5+1? I said, great idea. Let's just work on it.
And so, C5+1 was coined.
- More than a decade later, what are the main achievements of the C5+ format, particularly given that two U.S. presidents have met with Central Asian leaders to discuss political, economic, trade, and investment cooperation?
- So, the idea of Frederick Starr, under my personal kind of insistence with the State Department, we got this mechanism working. Now, after 2015, more than one decade has passed. It's interesting that it started as a ministerial level.
Today, it is already an institutionalized body with its own secretariat. It has different sector platforms on economy, energy, and issues, security. Lately, it was now C5+1 on minerals, rare earth minerals.
Again, there was an idea to work on the business component of it. It started with the United States Chamber of Commerce, and then it transformed itself into B5+1, a number of meetings of which were held in Astana.
From that moment on, the whole mechanism became more focused on the economy, trade and investment, connectivity, regional cooperation, AI development, and minerals. Now it has quite an extensive area of contacts and discussions.
What's interesting is that it started at the ministerial level. In 2025, it transformed into a summit meeting. It was in New York. President Trump invited all five Central Asian heads of state to the White House.
It was the first time this had been done at the White House. What's interesting, if we talk about Kazakhstan in particular, 29 agreements worth $17 billion were signed. Again, it shows that this mechanism is no longer at a nascent stage.
It's at a very active stage. Yes, now it's grown into a full-fledged mechanism of bilateral and regional cooperation with the countries of Central Asia. It's a thriving mechanism.
- Given the current geopolitical tensions and rising global conflicts, what challenges could these developments pose to the C5+ format and Central Asia’s efforts to strengthen dialogue and cooperation with its global partners?
- For me, one important thing I wanted to mention is that none of the other mechanisms we've created, like the US-Kazakhstan relationship over more than 17 years, stood the test of time.
The only one which is working and thriving today is the C5+1. We started during the Obama administration, and all the subsequent administrations supported it. Today, it has reached a much higher level. Of course, geopolitics plays its own role.
We understand that you cannot live in isolation from international issues. But it doesn't mean that we must be jeopardized by all those developments, because in the relationship between Central Asia and the US, we try to work on a positive agenda. Today, Central Asia is a region of stability and development.
So many issues are being resolved through the Coordination Council meetings among the heads of state. And it's a new development for Central Asia. Today, we are working in a very close, cooperative manner.
Of course, I gave you the figures. In general, the US presence in Kazakhstan is quite substantial. More than 600 US companies work in Kazakhstan. US investments today exceed $100 billion. Trade has also doubled in recent years, reaching $5 billion, which shows that we have so many positive things to work on. AI and digitalization, for example, are new trends in the world.
Of course, we discuss issues of stability. This is very important. It's a key issue. We're talking about threats and challenges which could pose a threat to Kazakhstan or Central Asia. Afghanistan is in a difficult situation, and we must take care of it as well. But in general, we try to discuss practical ways to cooperate to avoid and overcome those challenges through cooperation.
I think that, of course, there are some challenges and some issues. But in our discussions, we're mostly focusing today on the development agenda, regional integration, regional coordination, and connectivity.
And this is very much reflected here at the UN. At the UN, countries increasingly look at Central Asia as a united region, which is becoming a close unit, so to say. They see the countries as united in their initiatives, in what they propose, and in their willingness to build peace.
Because without peace, it's very difficult to talk about development. And if you don't work on development, you probably cannot have peace. So, these are two very interconnected things. We try to work not in a fragmented way, but with an understanding that there is a nexus between peace and security and sustainable development.
- How do you see the future of the C5+ format, particularly in light of rapid advances in digitalization and artificial intelligence? How might the mechanism evolve to address emerging opportunities and challenges?
- It's already a working mechanism. As I've said, it's digitalized. It has its own agenda, and it's working actively on the mutually beneficial issues for Central Asia and the United States. So, I see the future as the possibility through this mechanism to have a close collaboration among business circles, on economy, on artificial intelligence, on regional connectivity, which are very important for Central Asia.
That shows that this mechanism has quite a good future, because there's a lot of willingness to work, and there are some other countries, I know, that would like to have the same mechanism to work with Central Asian countries. So, it's a very promising future.
And, of course, during that time, it was not only this mechanism. For example, looking back, it was quite an interesting time for me because, during that time, we signed the agreement on a 10-year reciprocal visa regime with the United States.
There were many interesting developments during that time, and I would say it was good for Kazakhstan to start this kind of initiative, to work cooperatively with other Central Asian countries and our American colleagues on this idea. It's transforming itself, expanding, and making a lot of good starts and developments.
So, in general, to my mind, if we continue in the same way, the future is limitless. You know, there's B5+1 and the dialogue on minerals, the latest one, and I think that with every passing year, more areas are being added that could be of mutual benefit to all of us. We also have various other mechanisms, and all those mechanisms are working for the well-being of the peoples of Central Asia.

articles.title: India’s Russian oil in focus as Rubio visits major Reliance refinery - Inquirer.net
articles.summary: India’s Russian oil in focus as Rubio visits major Reliance refinery  Inquirer.net
articles.full_text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio kicks off a three-day visit to India on Monday in the finance hub of Mumbai, before heading to Jamnagar, home to a major oil refinery owned by industrial titan Reliance Industries.
Rubio’s business-oriented visit comes as trade talks remain stalled amid continued ambiguity on punitive measures from the US over India’s purchases of Russian oil.
Reliance is a top buyer of Venezuelan oil. The refinery can process 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, so it’s a valuable exporter of diesel fuel for global markets. The refinery has also been a major buyer of Russian Urals crude, making it a significant part of India’s energy relationship with Russia.
In March, Washington unveiled plans for a new oil refinery in Texas, backed by Reliance.
READ: US goes on the offensive in central Asia
US President Donald Trump has put the value of the project at $300 billion (€258 billion) and presented it as a way to help reduce the US trade deficit with India. Whether the project moves forward, and on what terms, will be closely watched.
An elusive US-India trade deal
Since taking office for a second time in 2025, Trump has gone back and forth on tariff threats with India over what he considers to be unfair trade practices, along with India’s continued purchases of Russian oil amid the war in Ukraine.
In February 2026, Trump announced a “trade deal” that slashed US tariffs on Indian goods, in exchange for India lowering trade barriers and halting purchases of Russian oil. Trump had claimed that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi promised to stop buying Russian oil. However, this has never been confirmed by New Delhi.
While maritime data from Kpler, a commodities and energy-market intelligence company, showed Indian refiners briefly diversified supply away from Russia to avoid tightening sanctions, India’s deep reliance on discounted Russian crude continues to be a cornerstone of its energy strategy. Russia remains India’s top supplier of crude oil.
In mid-September, Trump signed the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act,” imposing 100% tariffs on top buyers of Russian oil and gas, which includes India.
However, last week, just days before the legislation was due to go into effect, Trump signed an executive order pausing the sanctions.
Rubio: Trade deal ‘very close’
Before traveling to India, Rubio was in Uzbekistan for a meeting of the “C5+1” diplomatic platform comprising the US and five Central Asian countries. In remarks on the sidelines, Rubio said trade talks with India are taking place with the sanctions waivers in mind.
“We have had to waive sanctions over the past few months, looking at the global supplies, looking at global prices, and the impact it was having on other countries,” he said.
READ: Rubio open to Russia, China meets on PH visit
“We’re trying to finalize a trade deal with India right now. We’re very close to doing that,” Rubio added.
In an interview with Indian broadcaster NDTV, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said that Jamnagar could be a valuable source of diesel for the US.
Foreign policy analyst C Raja Mohan of Jindal Global University in India told DW that Rubio skipping a visit to the Indian capital in favor of Mumbai and Jamnagar should not be considered a diplomatic snub, as the refinery has international importance amid the global energy crunch brought on by the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
He said Jamnagar is an “important node in global trade” because it processes Russian oil and serves as a conduit for refined Russian petroleum products reaching Western markets.
Although Trump’s sanctions reprieve offers New Delhi temporary relief, the underlying threat remains. Washington retains the option of imposing punitive tariffs, leaving Russian oil as a potential source of leverage in wider trade negotiations.
Former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautioned against reading too much into Rubio’s decision to skip Delhi amid political criticism in India.
“The focus of his current trip is on energy, and he is visiting the Reliance refinery in Jamnagar,” she told DW. “The high price of fuel, particularly diesel, has become a political liability for the Trump administration, which wants to be seen taking action on this issue.”
Diesel prices have skyrocketed around the world following the Iran war and the ensuing disruption of supply from the Middle East. In waiving Russia sanctions, Trump has tried to blame Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities as being the cause of high prices.
Shankar pointed to Reliance’s proposed Texas refinery, noting that the state is “one of the states in play” in the upcoming midterm elections in the US.
“Some forward movement on the investment would be welcome,” she said.
Trump eroding trust in Delhi?
The two governments continue to describe their ties as a comprehensive global strategic partnership spanning defence, trade, technology and energy.
Analyst Mohan argued that describing the US-India relationship as uniquely transactional was misleading.
“Every nation ultimately acts out of national self-interest, rather than pure altruism or shared values,” he said.
The current friction, in his view, is part of a normal negotiation between two sovereign powers, not proof that the partnership was failing.
Besides Russian oil, another potential area of complication is the Trump administration suspending a scheme allowing US companies to sponsor skilled foreign workers.
On October 8, the Trump administration suspended new and pending applications under the US Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program at several technology companies amid investigations into alleged visa fraud and the displacement of US workers.
The process is a key step for employers seeking permanent residency for foreign staff, including Indian professionals.
Harsh Pant, vice president for studies and foreign policy at the Delhi-based Observer Research Foundation (ORF), said Trump’s own words and actions had damaged ties despite regular high-level engagement.
“Even as he calls Prime Minister Modi a good friend, he has damaged the relationship by targeting India, and his supporters have been targeting Indians,” Pant told DW.
Pant said inconsistent messaging from Washington was eroding trust and could have consequences well beyond Trump’s presidency.
“The sense that America is unreliable, that America can’t be trusted, is beginning to come back into policy discourse,” he said.
The damage, he warned, could reach beyond government-to-government relations to Indian students, professionals and the middle class, whose goodwill has helped sustain ties through earlier disagreements.
“If public sentiment goes against a country, then it becomes very difficult for the policy-makers to craft an alternative policy,” Pant said, adding that US actions affecting Indian students and professionals “will have consequences.” /dl

articles.title: Exclusive Interview: Analyst on Why Rubio’s Uzbekistan Visit Matters for US Strategy in Central Asia - Vision Times
articles.summary: Exclusive Interview: Analyst on Why Rubio’s Uzbekistan Visit Matters for US Strategy in Central Asia  Vision Times
articles.full_text:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was on a diplomatic visit to Uzbekistan from Oct. 18-20 to strengthen economic and strategic ties with the nations of Central Asia. The visit led to the signing of $12 billion worth of U.S.–Uzbekistan economic agreements and proposed projects.
Uzbekistan also became the 77th country on Monday (Oct. 20) to sign the Artemis Accords with the Trump administration. The Accords are a U.S.-led international framework for peaceful and responsible space exploration and were signed between Rubio and Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov.
Rubio also met his counterparts from five Central Asian nations in Samarkand — Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan — on Monday which according to Reuters was projected by U.S. officials as an opportunity to project its soft power in the region.
“I mean, look, it’s competition,” Rubio told journalists after a walk through the Registan Square that boasts of three massive, blue-tiled madrassas that date to the Timurid Empire. “We have products, we have companies, they make things, and we just want fair competition and an opportunity.”
Vision Times reporter Venus Upadhayaya talked about Rubio’s recent Central Asian visit with Syrian born Dr. Waiel Awwad, a Senior International Journalist and Political Analyst who has served in several global media houses including in senior roles in Al Arabiya and Middle East Broadcasting Center [MBC].

Dr. Awwad highlighted the trip as a “renewed” effort by the U.S. to increase its strategic interests in a region geopolitically saddled between Russia and China.
Venus Upadhayaya (Vision Times): How do you analyze Rubio’s recent visit to Uzbekistan and what does it indicate about U.S. policy in Central Asia?
Dr. Waiel Awwad: The USA has been eying CIS countries for decades. In fact, even the war on Afghanistan was part of the American strategy to gain access to CIS and use corridors for transferring of oil and gas from these rich countries.
Let us remember that American interest in Central Asia did not begin with Marco Rubio’s visit. It goes back to the 1990s, when Washington was already pursuing energy corridors designed to connect Caspian oil and gas to global markets while reducing dependence on routes controlled by Russia and avoiding Iran. The proposed Unocal pipeline through Afghanistan was part of that strategic and commercial landscape.
After 2001, the war created a new military and logistical dimension to America’s presence, while subsequent transport initiatives demonstrated the wider strategic importance of regional connectivity. We should be careful, however, not to claim that pipelines alone caused the invasion; the publicly documented reasons for the war centred on al-Qaeda and the Taliban’s provision of sanctuary to it.
So, Rubio’s engagement is not a new American discovery of Central Asia. It represents a renewed effort to secure commercial access, diversify critical-mineral supplies, develop transport corridors and maintain a strategic presence in a region where Russia and China already have substantial interests. What has changed is not Washington’s interest in Central Asia, but the intensity of the competition and the importance of critical minerals alongside oil, gas and transit routes.
Vision Times: Critical minerals have emerged as a priority for U.S.–Uzbekistan cooperation. How could this play out in Central Asia over the next five years?
Dr. Waiel Awwad: I see critical minerals becoming one of the main pillars of U.S. engagement with Central Asia over the next five years. The competition is not simply about extracting minerals; it is about controlling more of the supply chain, from exploration and mining to processing, refining and advanced manufacturing.
Uzbekistan and its neighbours possess deposits of minerals that may be important for batteries, electronics, renewable energy, aerospace and defence industries. For Washington, developing alternative sources of supply is also a way to reduce vulnerabilities associated with concentrated global processing and supply networks.
But the outcome will depend on whether U.S. companies are prepared to make long-term investments in infrastructure, technology transfer and local processing, rather than simply securing access to raw materials. Central Asian governments will want employment, industrial development, technical expertise and a larger share of the value generated from their resources.
Over the next five years, I expect stronger competition among American, Chinese, European, Russian, and other investors. Uzbekistan could emerge as an important hub, but geological potential alone does not guarantee commercial success. Water and energy availability, transport infrastructure, regulatory predictability and environmental standards will all matter.
The real question is whether Central Asia will remain a supplier of raw materials or become a centre for processing and higher-value industries. That distinction will determine how much lasting economic benefit the region gains from the critical-minerals race.
Vision Times: Rubio was accompanied by more than 100 U.S. companies and around 200 business executives. What do you make of this?
Dr. Waiel Awwad: This is a significant signal that Washington wants to move its relationship with Central Asia beyond diplomacy and security into the realm of long-term commercial engagement. The scale of the business delegation suggests that the United States sees opportunities in critical minerals, energy, aviation, agriculture, technology and transport infrastructure. The October 2026 C5+1 discussions also highlighted the Trans-Caspian trade corridor and industrial cooperation
Washington wants its companies to become long-term economic stakeholders in Central Asia. The countries of the region should welcome genuine investment, but evaluate every proposal on commercial viability, local benefits, technology transfer and the extent to which it strengthens their own productive capacity.
The objective should not be to replace one external dependency with another. It should be to create more choices.
Vision Times: Rubio said during his trip that the U.S. is not asking Central Asia to choose between powers. Is this realistic, or is Washington setting a narrative?
Dr. Waiel Awwad: That narrative can appeal to regional governments, but its credibility will depend on American behaviour. If Washington respects their independent choices and delivers commercially attractive partnerships, its message will carry weight. If economic cooperation becomes conditional on political alignment, the promise of strategic choice will become harder to sustain.
Central Asia’s response should be pragmatic: cooperate with Washington, maintain relations with Moscow and Beijing, and develop partnerships with Europe, India, Japan, South Korea and other interested economies.
For these countries, strategic autonomy is not about remaining equidistant from every power. It is about retaining the freedom to make decisions according to their national interests.
Vision Times: According to earlier reports, Trump plans to visit Uzbekistan (as mentioned by then-U.S. envoy for global partnerships Paolo Zampolli earlier this month). Why has Central Asia attracted this level of attention, and why is a possible Trump visit to Uzbekistan significant?
Dr. Waiel Awwad: Central Asia is attracting attention because several strategic developments are converging. It is rich in natural resources, occupies a pivotal position between Europe and Asia, and is increasingly important to the diversification of energy and mineral supply chains. Its transport corridors can connect markets across the Caspian region, while its growing economies offer opportunities in infrastructure, agriculture, manufacturing and technology.
The region also borders Russia, China, Afghanistan, and Iran, placing it at the intersection of several major security and economic questions. For Washington, engagement with Central Asia is therefore about more than bilateral commerce: it concerns the broader balance of influence across Eurasia.
Finally, Central Asia does not want to exchange one sphere of influence for another. It wants investment without dependency, partnerships without political subordination, and economic growth without being forced to choose sides. The power that understands this will build the most durable relationship with the region.

articles.title: Would replacing Zelenskyy change the war? - Türkiye Today
articles.summary: Would replacing Zelenskyy change the war?  Türkiye Today
articles.full_text:
President Trump's renewed pressure on Volodymyr Zelenskyy has brought Ukraine's leadership question back into focus. His latest call for another negotiator suggests that Washington increasingly regards the Ukrainian president as an obstacle to a settlement.
Yet replacing Zelenskyy would leave his successor facing much the same military problems and Russian demands.
The growing pressure for leadership change therefore raises a larger question about how much of Ukraine's war strategy any president can actually change.
The debate tends to intensify when military progress slows, or negotiations fail to produce results. Elections offer a possible way to renew political authority and allow those dissatisfied with Kyiv's approach to challenge its leadership.
4 million to 4.5 million voters remain abroad, with only 104 polling stations in consulates. Soldiers at the front and voters in occupied territories present further problems. A brief ceasefire would hardly resolve them.
Political competition inside Ukraine is nevertheless becoming more serious. Former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov's break with Zelenskyy, ex-commander-in-chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi’s popularity and the growing political influence of Zelenskyy’s chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, have weakened the president’s position.
Still, Zelenskyy retains considerable control over the government and can secure parliamentary support. His opponents have gained visibility without establishing a coalition capable of governing.
Growing dissatisfaction may therefore weaken the presidency before producing a credible replacement.
The strongest pressure for change may eventually come from the material costs of the war. Ukraine's persistent manpower problems complicate recruitment and prevent exhausted frontline units from receiving sufficient rest and replacements.
energy infrastructure are also reducing industrial output and tax revenues. These pressures may gradually increase public demands for a different approach to the war.
However, a new president would inherit the same shortage of trained personnel and the same need to finance the country's defense.
Zaluzhnyi's military reputation could give him greater authority to change mobilization policies or explain difficult compromises to the public.
His experience might also encourage him to resist territorial concessions that he considers militarily unnecessary. Neither outcome can be assumed. Military credibility could help a new president negotiate an agreement while making certain compromises politically harder to accept.
Ukrainian public opinion reinforces this uncertainty. A September survey found that 69% Ukrainian would accept a ceasefire along the existing front line if Ukraine retained the ability to strengthen its army and pursue EU and NATO membership, without legally recognizing occupied territory as Russian.
constitution reserves decisions changing the country's territory for a nationwide referendum.
A new president might find it easier to negotiate a temporary military arrangement than a permanent territorial settlement.
Russia's objectives would also remain. Moscow continues to demand Ukrainian withdrawal from territories it claims but does not fully control, alongside restrictions on Ukraine's future security arrangements.
Whoever succeeds Zelenskyy would face the problem of protecting the country against another offensive while obtaining terms acceptable to Moscow.
Personal relations between leaders may influence negotiations, although the underlying disagreement concerns Ukraine's future military capacity and control of territory.
For Moscow, the election debate itself may offer advantages. Political competition could weaken Kyiv's cohesion or create disputes over the winner's authority.
Moscow could therefore benefit from continuing to question Zelenskyy's authority even if replacing him offered no guarantee of a more favorable settlement.
Washington has different interests. Trump seeks progress toward ending the war while facing domestic pressure over energy prices and the costs of American involvement.
The dispute over Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries illustrates how these concerns increasingly influence military decisions. Zelenskyy's offer to suspend refinery strikes for 30 days in exchange for Patriot interceptors shows how Washington can use essential military supplies to influence Kyiv's choices.
American pressure may nevertheless complicate the settlement it seeks. Reduced intelligence sharing or delayed air-defense supplies could weaken Ukraine's negotiating position, encouraging Moscow to believe that continued fighting might secure better terms.
Their dissatisfaction with Zelenskyy can temporarily overlap without giving them a common preferred outcome.
Ukraine's growing dependence on European financing adds another constraint to any political transition. Europe is providing much of Kyiv's financial support, yet American weapons remain important to its defense.
Funding also depends on parliamentary decisions and reforms required by international lenders. A newly elected president would inherit a parliament chosen in 2019 and might lack a reliable majority.
Even a popular successor could struggle to maintain the flow of resources while reorganizing the government.
Russia faces mounting costs of its own as its defense expenditure continues to increase alongside fiscal pressure, although higher energy revenues help sustain the war effort.
For now, Zelenskyy appears more likely to remain in office while adjusting his policies and sharing more influence within the government.
A leadership transition would become more plausible if military and economic pressures continued to weaken his position, political rivals formed an effective coalition and a sustained ceasefire allowed credible elections.
Whether the resulting government could govern effectively would depend on its relationship with parliament, the military and Ukraine's foreign supporters.
Ukraine may eventually replace Zelenskyy before reaching a durable peace. Such a change could open new political possibilities, but the forces shaping the war would remain largely intact.
The question of who governs Ukraine is becoming more urgent, while the question of what that government can realistically achieve remains considerably harder to answer.

articles.title: Deeper China-Central Asia cooperation offers new opportunities for SCO development, says Tajik expert - Xinhua
articles.summary: Deeper China-Central Asia cooperation offers new opportunities for SCO development, says Tajik expert  Xinhua
articles.full_text:
DUSHANBE, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- Further deepening cooperation between China and Central Asian countries will create new opportunities for the development of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), a Tajik expert said.
In recent years, China and Central Asian countries have strengthened cooperation and achieved fruitful results in a number of areas, said Guzel Maitdinova, director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University, in a recent interview with Xinhua.
One of the key indicators of these achievements is the growth in trade volume between China and the five Central Asian countries -- Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and Turkmenistan, which exceeded 100 billion U.S. dollars in 2025 for the first time, Maitdinova noted.
Furthermore, regular political dialogue has been established, transport connectivity has expanded, industrial and technological cooperation has developed, and environmental and humanitarian issues have become part of the shared agenda, she added.
"For the SCO, deeper China-Central Asia ties create opportunities to broaden the organization's cooperation agenda by linking security with economic development, digital transformation, energy, environmental sustainability and human capital development," the expert said.
Maitdinova cited Chinese President Xi Jinping's remarks at the SCO summit in Bishkek in September, where he described the organization as "a priority area for promoting high-quality Belt and Road cooperation and implementing the Global Development Initiative."
She said the SCO provides a political and institutional platform for coordinating interests, while the Belt and Road Initiative promotes cooperation through infrastructure projects, investment and trade. Together, they create opportunities to develop cross-border transport corridors, energy networks, digital infrastructure and production chains.
Amid profound changes in the international landscape, the SCO is playing an increasingly important role in coordinating interests across Eurasia and advancing multilateral diplomacy, Maitdinova said.
At the Bishkek summit, Xi called for putting development first, taking security as a key goal, adopting a people-centered approach and promoting dialogue and consultation.
"These priorities reflect the SCO's role in strengthening regional security, promoting economic connectivity and maintaining dialogue among countries with different political and economic priorities," she said.
This year marks the 25th anniversary of the founding of the SCO. As Maitdinova pointed out, over the past quarter-century, the organization has developed a multilayered system of intergovernmental cooperation in which security issues are addressed in conjunction with economic development and people-to-people exchanges.
In her view, amid profound changes in the international situation, the SCO has evolved not only into a platform for regional dialogue and security coordination, but also into a significant mechanism for reconciling the interests of states in the emerging multipolar world order.
Maitdinova described the "Shanghai Spirit" as both the guiding principle of the SCO and a distinctive model of intergovernmental relations that emerged as countries in the region sought new mechanisms for security and cooperation.
The Shanghai Spirit embodies six principles -- mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, consultation, respect for diversity of civilizations, and pursuit of common development.
These principles provide a basis for cooperation among countries with different political systems, levels of economic development and foreign policy priorities, Maitdinova said.
Guided by the Shanghai Spirit, the SCO continues to develop and strengthen, helping translate multilateral dialogue into concrete results in cooperation among member states, she added. ■

articles.title: World Insights: China-Central Asia cooperation boosts SCO development - India's News.Net
articles.summary: World Insights: China-Central Asia cooperation boosts SCO development  India's News.Net
articles.full_text:
DUSHANBE, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- During his just-concluded official visits to Uzbekistan and Tajikistan and attendance at the 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (Prime Ministers) of Member States of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), Chinese Premier Li Qiang called for closer cooperation with the two Central Asian countries and greater development of the SCO.
In recent years, China has deepened practical cooperation with Central Asian countries and injected fresh momentum into development of the SCO by enhancing connectivity, trade and exchanges in various fields. Analysts say these efforts will contribute to common prosperity and high-quality development in the region and beyond.
CONNECTIVITY BRINGS OPPORTUNITY
Enhancing connectivity between China and the landlocked countries of Central Asia is key to promoting development in the region and beyond. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, now under construction, is a prime example of this effort.
In recent years, the railway project has remained high on the agenda of leaders of the countries involved. Most recently, during Li's official visit to Uzbekistan, the two sides pledged to advance the railway's high-quality construction.
The railway, launched at the end of 2024, is a flagship project of the Belt and Road Initiative, serving as a strategic link between China and Central Asia. The route will begin in Kashgar in northwest China and pass through the mountainous terrain of Kyrgyzstan to reach Uzbekistan.
High-quality construction and efficient operation of the railway will set a valuable example for countries across the region and beyond, said Kubanychbek Taabaldiev, a professor at Ala-Too International University in Bishkek.
"It has the potential to change the economic geography of Central Asia and transform Kyrgyzstan from a country located between major markets into an important link between China, Central Asia, and further on to European and Middle Eastern destinations," Taabaldiev said.
Beyond railway and road construction, the strengthening of transport cooperation between China and Central Asian countries also encompasses facilitating customs clearance at borders, digitizing transport permits and other efficiency-enhancing measures. Better connectivity has created new development opportunities for the region, boosting trade and exchanges in various fields.
Ulugbek Shermatov, chairman of the Committee on International Affairs, Defence and Security of the Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis of Uzbekistan, noted that the creation of new transport arteries "not only expands economic opportunities, but also forms a solid material foundation for long-term interdependence and peaceful cooperation in the region."
This demonstrates China's commitment to developing friendly relations with neighboring states and promoting Belt and Road cooperation, Shermatov said.
PRACTICAL COOPERATION BEARS FRUIT
From trade and agriculture to cutting-edge technological innovation, practical cooperation between China and Central Asia has been a driving force behind regional growth and, more broadly, the development of the SCO as a whole.
Trade figures speak to the robust momentum in cooperation. China's trade with five Central Asian countries topped 100 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, hitting a record high. Meanwhile, trade structure continues to improve, with more Central Asian products entering the Chinese market.
"Stability in the region is inextricably linked with trade and economic development. The growth of the total trade turnover of Central Asian countries with China ... clearly demonstrates China's importance in ensuring stability in our region," said Shermatov.
Building on traditional merchandise trade, both sides are further expanding cooperation in digital trade, agriculture, energy, manufacturing, as well as scientific and technological innovation.
Take energy cooperation as an example. Cooperation has gradually expanded from traditional oil and gas to clean energy and related technologies.
At the Second China-Central Asia Summit in Astana, Kazakhstan last year, China and the five Central Asian nations pledged to support the establishment of a China-Central Asia energy development partnership to expand cooperation across the entire energy industry chains.
The countries also affirmed their commitment to promoting technological and talent exchanges and cooperation in areas such as the management and development of desertified and saline-alkali lands.
"China possesses rich technical expertise in renewable energy, electric mobility, digital infrastructure, telecommunications, artificial intelligence (AI) and industrial automation," said Mukhtor Umarov, chairman of the Economic Assembly of Uzbekistan.
At the broader SCO level, the establishment and development of cooperation platforms between China and other SCO members in emerging fields "have opened new avenues for countries in the region -- shifting the focus from simply purchasing equipment toward technology localization, joint R&D, engineer cultivation and the buildout of new production capacities," Umarov said.
SCO DEVELOPMENT STRENGTHENED
Leaders of China and Central Asian nations, together with their SCO colleagues, reaffirmed stronger cooperation within the SCO framework at the just-concluded 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (Prime Ministers) of Member States of the SCO in the Tajik capital of Dushanbe.
China's coordination with Central Asia will help promote the high-quality development of the SCO by strengthening the foundation for regional security, expanding economic cooperation and connectivity, and cementing mutual trust among member states.
These efforts will further enhance the SCO's role in safeguarding regional security, promoting common development and improving global governance, experts said.
"In my view, the most prominent feature of China's current contribution to the development of the SCO lies in its tight integration of strategic concepts, multilateral rules and concrete development tools," said Uzbek expert Umarov.
"Against the backdrop of intensifying geoeconomic fragmentation, increasing trade restrictions, and chronic shortages of long-term financing, SCO member states urgently need predictable rules and institutions to mitigate risks faced by enterprises," he said.
China has been a key contributor to the SCO's evolution. At the Tianjin Summit last year, a milestone in the SCO's development, China and other member states jointly formulated a development strategy for the organization for the next decade and action plans to promote high-quality development.
Since the Tianjin Summit, a number of cooperation platforms have been launched, covering green industry, digital economy, scientific and technological innovation, energy, education and AI.
At the Bishkek Summit earlier this year, China brought more initiatives and projects supporting the SCO's development, including the establishment of a China-SCO port economic cooperation center in Tianjin, the launch of an international AI application cooperation center, and the training of more green industry professionals.
The SCO's international significance is "determined not only by its geographical reach or the combined potential of its member states, but also by its ability to translate political agreements into functioning mechanisms for security, economic cooperation, and diplomatic coordination," said Guzel Maitdinova, director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University.
"Looking ahead, linking SCO economic initiatives with national development strategies, China's Belt and Road Initiative, and the programs of international financial institutions could play a particularly important role," Maitdinova added.
Shermatov, meanwhile, offered an Uzbek perspective: "This is precisely how we see the responsibility of China and Uzbekistan for the future of the SCO -- to preserve the Shanghai Spirit while simultaneously adapting the organization to new global realities."

articles.title: Deterring China Without Alienating Russia - American Thinker
articles.summary: Deterring China Without Alienating Russia  American Thinker
articles.full_text:
Ken Moriyasu, senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, recently posted an article titled ‘ Why Losing a Taiwan War Might Not Break China,” in which he raised the question of whether strengthening U.S. influence in Central Asia would deter Beijing from attacking Taiwan or encourage China to accelerate its military preparations and deepen its partnership with Russia.
Moriyasu argues that China’s growing economic and strategic connections throughout Eurasia could enable it to cope with the effects of a failed invasion of Taiwan by decreasing its reliance on vulnerable sea routes. As a countermeasure, strengthened U.S. ties with the Central Asian states could complicate Beijing's strategic assessment and make military action against Taiwan less appealing.
This strategy, however, carries a danger. If Chinese leaders perceive an expanded U.S. presence in Central Asia as an attempt at strategic encirclement, they may accelerate military preparations, stockpile essential resources, and deepen cooperation with Moscow. China and Russia already share an interest in limiting American influence, while their military exercises, energy trade, and defense-industrial cooperation have strengthened their relationship. Pressure on China could therefore consolidate the partnership Washington hopes to weaken.
The answer, however, may lie in a lesson from Richard Nixon’s presidency. Rather than confronting Moscow and Beijing as an inseparable bloc, Washington should explore whether engagement with Russia could exploit differences between the two powers and improve America’s strategic position.
Nixon’s trip to China in 1972 provides a historical example of this kind of strategy. Taking advantage of the deep division between China and the Soviet Union, which had reached a climax with armed border clashes in 1969, Nixon and his National Security Advisor, Henry Kissinger, pursued rapprochement with Beijing in order to change Moscow’s strategic assessments. Their aim was not to form an alliance based on common political values, but rather to use the conflicting interests of the two communist countries to increase American diplomatic influence. The fact that contact had been established with China showed that Washington could enhance its position by dealing with one of its rivals instead of viewing both of them as a single opposing force.
The current situation is not the same. Since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russia and China have developed a much closer strategic relationship; Beijing gives Moscow significant economic assistance, and both governments oppose certain elements of the U.S.-led international order. However, Russia and China do not share identical strategic interests. Moscow has reasons for resisting too great a dependence on Beijing, as the latter’s growing economic influence is having an increasing effect on their relationship, and Russia still has longstanding interests in Central Asia, since Chinese commercial expansion may come into competition with Russian influence.
Washington should consider whether these differences create opportunities for selective engagement; possible avenues for dialogue could include nuclear risk reduction, arms-control talks, questions of regional security, and carefully defined economic cooperation. The aim would not be to turn Russia into an American ally all at once, but rather to offer Moscow alternatives to its increasingly asymmetric relationship with Beijing.
Recent developments make this possibility particularly relevant. On October 16, President Donald Trump signed an executive order waiving significant sanctions, restrictions, and tariffs provided for under the newly enacted Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act. The order cited the national interest and left the waivers in effect until further action was deemed appropriate.
The order followed Trump’s announcement of an agreement with Vladimir Putin under which Russia would release diesel supplies to global markets to ease fuel-price pressures. The deal drew criticism from lawmakers in both parties and from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who argued that easing restrictions could benefit Moscow while its war against Ukraine continued.
These developments demonstrate the extent to which transactional diplomacy both can and cannot achieve. While negotiations with Moscow concerning energy supplies may lead to openings in other fields, a commercial agreement does not serve as evidence of a strategic realignment, and a sanctions waiver does not show that Russia desires to decouple from China. If Washington relaxes economic pressure without making substantial concessions, it is effectively giving up its leverage rather than creating a geopolitical opening.
When dealing with Moscow, it is necessary to base any approach on a realistic evaluation of the war in Ukraine. Since Ukraine is suffering from a lack of manpower, there is reason to doubt its capacity to secure a decisive military victory. It follows that the U.S. ought to engage in diplomacy which safeguards Ukrainian sovereignty and at the same time aims at reaching a negotiated agreement, rather than continuing the conflict without a realistic prospect of winning. Moreover, the U.S. must not respond in a way that rewards Russian aggression or allow it to gain a sphere of influence over the former Soviet republics.
This principle should also be the basis of American policy towards Central Asia. The countries in the region should be left free to decide for themselves their political, economic, and security arrangements. The Trump administration ought to promote their independence through investment, energy diversification, infrastructure development, and diplomatic cooperation, rather than pressuring them to align exclusively with the United States, Russia, or China.
In the end, while increasing American influence in Central Asia could help in deterring China, it still cannot take the place of real military preparedness and cooperation with Indo-Pacific partners. Likewise, Washington should avoid turning strategic competition into a contest that gives Moscow and Beijing ever stronger reasons to cooperate.
Nixon did not make China a trusted partner of America; rather, he saw strategic value in divisions among rival powers and used diplomacy to shift the balance of power.
Washington must decide whether it can regain that strategic flexibility. If it combines a credible deterrent posture around Taiwan, maintains ongoing engagement with Central Asia, and pursues carefully conditioned diplomacy with Moscow, it could make Chinese aggression less appealing while reducing incentives for a growing Sino-Russian alignment. The aim should not be to pick Russia over China, but to stop Beijing and Moscow from thinking their interests are best advanced by acting together against the United States.

articles.title: [不同来源] World Insights: China-Central Asia cooperation boosts SCO development - Malaysia Sun
articles.summary: World Insights: China-Central Asia cooperation boosts SCO development  Malaysia Sun
articles.full_text:
Xinhua
                
21 Oct 2026, 10:45 GMT+10
            
DUSHANBE, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- During his just-concluded official visits to Uzbekistan and Tajikistan and attendance at the 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (Prime Ministers) of Member States of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), Chinese Premier Li Qiang called for closer cooperation with the two Central Asian countries and greater development of the SCO.
In recent years, China has deepened practical cooperation with Central Asian countries and injected fresh momentum into development of the SCO by enhancing connectivity, trade and exchanges in various fields. Analysts say these efforts will contribute to common prosperity and high-quality development in the region and beyond.
CONNECTIVITY BRINGS OPPORTUNITY
Enhancing connectivity between China and the landlocked countries of Central Asia is key to promoting development in the region and beyond. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, now under construction, is a prime example of this effort.
In recent years, the railway project has remained high on the agenda of leaders of the countries involved. Most recently, during Li's official visit to Uzbekistan, the two sides pledged to advance the railway's high-quality construction.
The railway, launched at the end of 2024, is a flagship project of the Belt and Road Initiative, serving as a strategic link between China and Central Asia. The route will begin in Kashgar in northwest China and pass through the mountainous terrain of Kyrgyzstan to reach Uzbekistan.
High-quality construction and efficient operation of the railway will set a valuable example for countries across the region and beyond, said Kubanychbek Taabaldiev, a professor at Ala-Too International University in Bishkek.
"It has the potential to change the economic geography of Central Asia and transform Kyrgyzstan from a country located between major markets into an important link between China, Central Asia, and further on to European and Middle Eastern destinations," Taabaldiev said.
Beyond railway and road construction, the strengthening of transport cooperation between China and Central Asian countries also encompasses facilitating customs clearance at borders, digitizing transport permits and other efficiency-enhancing measures. Better connectivity has created new development opportunities for the region, boosting trade and exchanges in various fields.
Ulugbek Shermatov, chairman of the Committee on International Affairs, Defence and Security of the Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis of Uzbekistan, noted that the creation of new transport arteries "not only expands economic opportunities, but also forms a solid material foundation for long-term interdependence and peaceful cooperation in the region."
This demonstrates China's commitment to developing friendly relations with neighboring states and promoting Belt and Road cooperation, Shermatov said.
PRACTICAL COOPERATION BEARS FRUIT
From trade and agriculture to cutting-edge technological innovation, practical cooperation between China and Central Asia has been a driving force behind regional growth and, more broadly, the development of the SCO as a whole.
Trade figures speak to the robust momentum in cooperation. China's trade with five Central Asian countries topped 100 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, hitting a record high. Meanwhile, trade structure continues to improve, with more Central Asian products entering the Chinese market.
"Stability in the region is inextricably linked with trade and economic development. The growth of the total trade turnover of Central Asian countries with China ... clearly demonstrates China's importance in ensuring stability in our region," said Shermatov.
Building on traditional merchandise trade, both sides are further expanding cooperation in digital trade, agriculture, energy, manufacturing, as well as scientific and technological innovation.
Take energy cooperation as an example. Cooperation has gradually expanded from traditional oil and gas to clean energy and related technologies.
At the Second China-Central Asia Summit in Astana, Kazakhstan last year, China and the five Central Asian nations pledged to support the establishment of a China-Central Asia energy development partnership to expand cooperation across the entire energy industry chains.
The countries also affirmed their commitment to promoting technological and talent exchanges and cooperation in areas such as the management and development of desertified and saline-alkali lands.
"China possesses rich technical expertise in renewable energy, electric mobility, digital infrastructure, telecommunications, artificial intelligence (AI) and industrial automation," said Mukhtor Umarov, chairman of the Economic Assembly of Uzbekistan.
At the broader SCO level, the establishment and development of cooperation platforms between China and other SCO members in emerging fields "have opened new avenues for countries in the region -- shifting the focus from simply purchasing equipment toward technology localization, joint R&D, engineer cultivation and the buildout of new production capacities," Umarov said.
SCO DEVELOPMENT STRENGTHENED
Leaders of China and Central Asian nations, together with their SCO colleagues, reaffirmed stronger cooperation within the SCO framework at the just-concluded 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (Prime Ministers) of Member States of the SCO in the Tajik capital of Dushanbe.
China's coordination with Central Asia will help promote the high-quality development of the SCO by strengthening the foundation for regional security, expanding economic cooperation and connectivity, and cementing mutual trust among member states.
These efforts will further enhance the SCO's role in safeguarding regional security, promoting common development and improving global governance, experts said.
"In my view, the most prominent feature of China's current contribution to the development of the SCO lies in its tight integration of strategic concepts, multilateral rules and concrete development tools," said Uzbek expert Umarov.
"Against the backdrop of intensifying geoeconomic fragmentation, increasing trade restrictions, and chronic shortages of long-term financing, SCO member states urgently need predictable rules and institutions to mitigate risks faced by enterprises," he said.
China has been a key contributor to the SCO's evolution. At the Tianjin Summit last year, a milestone in the SCO's development, China and other member states jointly formulated a development strategy for the organization for the next decade and action plans to promote high-quality development.
Since the Tianjin Summit, a number of cooperation platforms have been launched, covering green industry, digital economy, scientific and technological innovation, energy, education and AI.
At the Bishkek Summit earlier this year, China brought more initiatives and projects supporting the SCO's development, including the establishment of a China-SCO port economic cooperation center in Tianjin, the launch of an international AI application cooperation center, and the training of more green industry professionals.
The SCO's international significance is "determined not only by its geographical reach or the combined potential of its member states, but also by its ability to translate political agreements into functioning mechanisms for security, economic cooperation, and diplomatic coordination," said Guzel Maitdinova, director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University.
"Looking ahead, linking SCO economic initiatives with national development strategies, China's Belt and Road Initiative, and the programs of international financial institutions could play a particularly important role," Maitdinova added.
Shermatov, meanwhile, offered an Uzbek perspective: "This is precisely how we see the responsibility of China and Uzbekistan for the future of the SCO -- to preserve the Shanghai Spirit while simultaneously adapting the organization to new global realities."

articles.title: From Samarkand to Washington: New Economic Opportunities in Uzbekistan–U.S. Cooperation - EIN News
articles.summary: From Samarkand to Washington: New Economic Opportunities in Uzbekistan–U.S. Cooperation  EIN News
articles.full_text:
Political trust, investment and advanced technologies mark a new stage in the strategic partnership.
TASHKENT, UZBEKISTAN, October 20, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- The Samarkand dialogue held on October 19, 2026, marked an important opportunity to strengthen Uzbekistan–U.S. relations and expand cooperation between the United States and Central Asia. The participation of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio underscored the strategic importance of bilateral ties, with discussions focusing on trade, investment, industrial development, critical minerals, financial markets and advanced technologies.
The dialogue highlighted Uzbekistan’s growing role as a reliable international partner and a key link between Central Asia and global markets.
From Political Dialogue to Economic Results
A central priority in bilateral relations is translating political engagement into practical economic outcomes. The development of the Uzbekistan–U.S. Business and Investment Council is an important step towards strengthening direct contacts between governments, financial institutions and private-sector representatives, facilitating investment and addressing business challenges.
A total of 54 agreements and initiatives worth nearly $12 billion have been reported in connection with bilateral engagement. These initiatives reflect growing commercial interest and the potential to develop long-term partnerships.
For Uzbekistan, cooperation with the United States offers opportunities to attract capital, introduce advanced technologies and develop higher-value industries. American businesses, in turn, can access Uzbekistan’s expanding market and explore opportunities across Central Asia.
Trade and Investment on the Rise
Bilateral trade has grown significantly, increasing from approximately $215 million in 2017 to nearly $1 billion in 2025—around 4.7 times higher.
The positive trend continued in 2026. During the first eight months, bilateral trade reached $810.4 million, a 33.4 per cent increase compared with the same period in 2025. Uzbekistan’s exports to the United States amounted to $304.5 million, up 59.9 per cent, while imports from the United States totalled approximately $506 million, an increase of 21.3 per cent.
Further growth is possible in manufacturing, agriculture, energy, transport and information technology, where both countries can benefit from complementary capabilities.
Investment is another important pillar of the partnership. As of September 1, 2026, 377 companies with U.S. investment were operating in Uzbekistan. Between 2017 and 2025, the country attracted more than $2.9 billion in U.S. direct investment and loans.
These figures reflect expanding business engagement and the opportunities associated with Uzbekistan’s economic reforms, market development and efforts to improve the investment climate.
Financial Markets and Strategic Industries
The planned initial public offering of Uzbekistan’s National Investment Fund, valued at approximately $700 million, represents another step towards developing capital markets and attracting international investors.
The fund consolidates stakes in 13 state-owned enterprises, with international investment management company Franklin Templeton involved in its management. The initiative aims to strengthen corporate governance, improve transparency and promote more efficient asset management. Its success will depend on consistent implementation and sustained investor confidence.
Cooperation is also expanding into strategic industries, including critical minerals, advanced technologies, innovation and space-related activities.
Uzbekistan’s natural resources and geographical position create opportunities to develop mineral processing and supply chains for modern industries. For the United States, such cooperation can help diversify supply sources; for Uzbekistan, it offers the prospect of moving beyond raw-material exports towards higher-value production.
Technology partnerships can support industrial modernisation, digitalisation, skills development and the integration of Uzbek businesses into international value chains.
Uzbekistan’s accession to the Artemis Accords as the 77th signatory further demonstrates its interest in international cooperation on the peaceful exploration and use of outer space, creating potential opportunities for scientific exchange and technological development.
Strengthening Central Asia’s Global Position
The Uzbekistan–U.S. partnership also has a broader regional dimension. Improved connectivity, trade facilitation, infrastructure development and diversified economic partnerships are essential to Central Asia’s long-term prosperity.
Uzbekistan’s efforts to strengthen relations with neighbouring countries and expand international economic links can complement deeper engagement with the United States. Investment and commercial cooperation can support cross-border business activities, open new markets and strengthen the region’s integration into the global economy.
For international partners, a more connected and economically dynamic Central Asia offers opportunities for trade and investment. For regional countries, broader partnerships can diversify economic relations and support sustainable development.
The Samarkand dialogue therefore represents more than a diplomatic meeting: it provides a platform for advancing regional cooperation and strengthening Central Asia’s role in international economic relations.
Turning Commitments into Sustainable Results
The development of Uzbekistan–U.S. relations demonstrates a growing shift from political dialogue towards practical cooperation. Rising trade, expanding investment, new financial instruments and engagement in strategic industries provide a foundation for further progress.
The key indicators underline this potential: bilateral trade approached $1 billion in 2025; trade reached $810.4 million in the first eight months of 2026; 377 companies with U.S. investment operated in Uzbekistan as of September 1, 2026; and U.S. direct investment and loans attracted between 2017 and 2025 exceeded $2.9 billion. In addition, 54 agreements and initiatives valued at nearly $12 billion and the planned $700 million National Investment Fund IPO highlight the scale of economic ambitions.
Realising these opportunities will require transparent institutions, consistent reforms, effective implementation of agreements and stronger links between businesses.
By building on the momentum generated in Samarkand, Uzbekistan and the United States can deepen their strategic partnership, expand mutually beneficial economic cooperation and create new opportunities for investors, businesses and people across both countries and the wider Central Asian region.
