articles.title: Financial Street Forum highlights openness, win-win cooperation to advance high-quality BRI development - Global Times
articles.summary: Financial Street Forum highlights openness, win-win cooperation to advance high-quality BRI development  Global Times
articles.full_text:
Annual Conference of Financial Street Forum (FSF) 2026 in Beijing on October 20, 2026 Photo: Yin Yeping/GT
Chinese and foreign government officials and industry representatives highlighted the importance of openness, win-win cooperation and financial innovation in advancing high-quality Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) development at a parallel forum of the Annual Conference of Financial Street Forum 2026 in Beijing on Wednesday, calling for stronger international cooperation to expand investment and financing opportunities.
Under the theme "Upholding Openness and Win-Win Cooperation to Foster New Dynamism for High Quality Belt and Road Cooperation," the forum, co-organized by the Export-Import Bank of China (CEXIM), brought together representatives from China and BRI partner countries to discuss infrastructure connectivity, sustainable financing and new opportunities for economic cooperation.
As a major financial institution supporting the BRI, CEXIM has extended more than 7 trillion yuan ($1.04 trillion) in loans to support the initiative over the past decade, with operations covering more than 130 partner countries, Chen Huaiyu, chairperson of the bank, said at the forum.
Chen said that the bank has continued to promote financial innovation and cooperation, including establishing a 30-billion-yuan special financing quota for China-Europe freight trains and creating the market's first basket of panda bonds involving BRI partner countries.
The bank has also explored diversified cooperation models with institutions including the New Development Bank and the World Bank to amplify the impact of financing, he said.
The growing economic ties between China and BRI partner countries have also been reflected in Beijing's expanding trade with these markets.
Vice Mayor of Beijing Tang Wenhong said that the Beijing has actively explored international markets under the initiative and launched its first freight train service to Central Asia.
In 2025, Beijing's total trade reached 3.19 trillion yuan, of which trade with BRI partner countries accounted for 1.93 trillion yuan, or 60.4 percent of the total, according to Tang.
While Chinese officials highlighted progress in financial support and trade connectivity, representatives from African countries emphasized the need for more diversified and sustainable financing to translate infrastructure investment into long-term economic development.
Kenya's Cabinet Secretary for the National Treasury and Economic Planning John Mbadi Ng'ongo said in remarks delivered from a satellite venue that the BRI has emerged as an important framework for strengthening connectivity, facilitating trade and investment, and expanding access to development finance.
For Kenya, infrastructure remains a key pillar of its national development agenda, with investment needed in the transport, energy, water, information and communication technology, and other critical sectors.
Achieving these objectives requires strong partnerships and access to adequate, affordable and sustainable financing, Mbadi said.
He welcomed growing collaboration among African countries, China, multilateral development institutions and the private sector in mobilizing resources for major development projects, noting that such partnerships also provide opportunities for knowledge sharing, technology transfer, capacity building and deeper economic integration.
Echoing the call for stronger financial cooperation, Lesotho's Minister of Finance and Development Planning Retselisitsoe Matlanyane highlighted China's experience in gradually opening its financial system while strengthening domestic institutions, saying that it offers lessons for African countries seeking to expand financial inclusion and access to capital.
On cooperation under the BRI, she said that the initiative has provided an important platform for strengthening connectivity, expanding economic cooperation and developing trade corridors. Such cooperation should be aligned with national development priorities and deliver tangible benefits to local communities, she added.
At Wednesday's forum, CEXIM signed cooperation agreements with international financial institutions and enterprises, covering financial cooperation, industrial development and overseas investment.
The growing emphasis on financial cooperation under the BRI reflects a shift toward more diversified and sustainable financing models, particularly as partner countries seek to address infrastructure gaps and support long-term economic growth, Hu Qimu, professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, told the Global Times on Wednesday.
The expert said that closer cooperation among Chinese financial institutions, multilateral development banks and local partners could help mobilize more capital, share investment risks and improve the efficiency of project financing. Such cooperation could also help translate infrastructure connectivity into tangible economic benefits by facilitating trade, attracting investment and creating local jobs, the expert noted.

articles.title: German foundations leave Georgia: what the crisis in Berlin-Tbilisi relations means - JAMnews

articles.full_text:
Two German foundations, the Konrad Adenauer Foundation and the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, have ceased operations in Georgia, where they had worked for more than two decades.
The move follows the adoption of a law on grants that requires foreign foundations to obtain government permission to operate in Georgia. The two foundations failed to secure approval and announced their withdrawal from the country.
Two other German foundations, the Heinrich Böll Foundation and the Friedrich Ebert Foundation, have resumed operations after a pause — at least for now.
- EU to consider reviewing its policy towards Georgia: what will change in January?
- All four German political foundations halt work in Georgia; ALDE calls for EU sanctions
- Georgia’s new laws are destroying independent civil society groups, says Human Rights Watch
The problems facing German foundations in Georgia are not viewed in isolation. Instead, they are seen as another consequence of repressive legislation and a clear sign that relations between Tbilisi and Berlin have reached an impasse.
Germany was among the first countries to support Georgia and express solidarity with it in the early years after independence. However, relations between Georgia and Germany have deteriorated over the past several years.
The crisis deepened in 2024, when the Georgian government’s decision to suspend European integration, its adoption of repressive laws and its crackdown on protests drew sharp criticism from the German government.
The Georgian authorities responded by launching a campaign to discredit Germany’s ambassador and the country as a whole. Germany, in turn, imposed visa restrictions on some members of the ruling Georgian Dream party. It also suspended planned development projects worth €237 million with the Georgian government.
Germany is more than just a partner country for Georgia. It is one of the European Union’s most influential political players, while Georgia remains a candidate for EU membership. The deterioration in Georgian-German relations therefore goes beyond diplomatic disagreements.
What German foundations did in Georgia
All four German foundations had operated in Georgia since the early 2000s. Their aim was to support the country’s democratic development and strengthen civil society. They worked with government agencies, civil society organisations, young people, researchers, women and minority groups. Their activities covered a wide range of areas, and they implemented dozens of projects across the country that benefited hundreds of people.
Dea Metreveli, who holds a doctorate in philology, headed the state-run Book Centre for many years. She says it would have been very difficult for the centre to attend prestigious events such as the Frankfurt Book Fair without support from the German foundations. Georgia’s participation, which also brought Georgian authors to the fair, had been a major achievement.
“When we prepared for the fair in 2018, the foundations had already laid the groundwork for our participation. They helped us organise various events. Much of this tremendous success came from our cooperation with them,” Metreveli recalls.
Giorgi Butikashvili, a lecturer at Ilia State University, worked for 12 years as a programme manager at the South Caucasus office of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation.
He recalls, among other things, joint Georgian-Abkhaz projects and dialogue between religious communities. The foundation’s support made these initiatives possible. He says Georgian government agencies took part in all these projects.
“When projects involving Abkhaz participants began, for example, everything was coordinated with the Ministry of Reconciliation. We planned everything in line with the government’s strategy. Germany was not pursuing its own interests; it was helping Georgia pursue its national interests. The German government provided resources that the Georgian state itself lacked.”
Metreveli also remembers a specific project involving Abkhaz participants: a joint collection of works by contemporary Georgian and Abkhaz women writers, published in Georgian and Abkhaz. It was one of the last projects the Konrad Adenauer Foundation helped implement.
“Imagine a single book featuring four contemporary Georgian women writers alongside four Abkhaz women writers living in Sukhumi. They worked together for a year, discussed the concept of the publication together and became friends.”
The Soviet Past Research Laboratory (SOVLAB) also worked with all four German foundations at various times over many years. Irakli Khvadagiani, a historian and researcher at the organisation, says their support enabled SOVLAB to publish a range of works on the Soviet and Russian occupation, state terror and the stories of countless individuals.
“From 2012 onwards, the state effectively pursued a passive-aggressive approach. It had no agenda for memory politics. On the contrary, it left the door wide open to Russian disinformation. Then, from the late 2010s, the authorities moved into a more aggressive phase: attacks on us and civil society, and the closure of archives. Under these conditions, we were able to keep working largely thanks to these foundations.”
Khvadagiani says the foundations helped fill the vacuum that the Russian regime was creating in the fields of historical memory, research and the teaching of contemporary history. None of this work would have been possible without the support of Germany’s partners.
Beyond the foundations’ work in Georgia itself, the German government also supported hundreds of young Georgians in pursuing higher education in Germany. One of them is Mamuka Andguladze, chair of the Media Advocacy Coalition. Funding from Germany’s DAAD programme enabled him to earn a doctorate in media law in Germany.
“It was very important to me to have the opportunity to study in Germany. Hundreds of young people had the same opportunity. And what happened to the knowledge they gained? They brought it back to our country. You get an education and return home to help build better institutions, a better court system and better elections.”
Why the problem facing the foundations is about more than the foundations themselves
Tina Khidasheli, Georgia’s former defence minister and now head of the organisation Civic IDEA, believes the problems facing German foundations should not be viewed solely as a consequence of repressive legislation.
In her view, this is the first clear sign of deteriorating relations between Georgia and Germany. She says Germany has historically played a key role in the development of the Georgian state, dating back to the early 20th century. Georgia’s state institutions are rooted in German legislation, law and institutional structures. Politicians from successive generations have attached particular importance to relations with Germany, making the current situation unprecedented.
For Giorgi Butikashvili, the situation clearly confirms an attempt to consolidate autocratic rule in Georgia.
“The closure of foreign foundations was the final stage in Russia, Belarus and Azerbaijan, when the authorities decided to consolidate autocracy once and for all. This is a symptom of autocratic regimes,” Butikashvili stresses.
What does the tension with Berlin mean for Tbilisi?
According to Irakli Khvadagiani, the crisis in relations with Germany means that Georgia remains behind an Iron Curtain.
“This is a continuation of the imperialist and aggressive policy Russia pursued, including during the Soviet era. Its sphere of influence — the territory it claims, which it sees as encompassing much of Eurasia — must remain behind an Iron Curtain. No outside influence, no ties, no cooperation.”
Tina Khidasheli, meanwhile, does not believe the Georgian Dream government singled out Germany in particular. She points out that its representatives have used similar rhetoric against other European countries. Nevertheless, she sees this as a dangerous sign.
“We are talking about a country that belongs to the G7. A country that is the strongest economically, or by any other measure. Moreover, since Brexit, Germany has become the most important player in the European Union. It carries the greatest weight internationally when it comes to European policy,” Khidasheli says.
She recalls that Germany blocked Georgia’s path towards NATO membership in 2008. It is therefore logical and natural that Georgia’s state policy has always aimed to establish and maintain good relations with Berlin.
“Germany’s veto, Germany’s opposition, mean that we have no chance not only of joining any future round of enlargement, but even of establishing serious relations with either the European Union or NATO.”
Meanwhile, relations between Georgia and Germany have reached an impasse despite the fact that several senior Georgian officials built their professional careers in Germany.
From 2003 to 2020, Georgian Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili worked for the German Agency for Technical Cooperation (GTZ) and the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ), including as head of the Georgian team.
Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze earned a doctorate in law at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf.
Another Georgian Dream member, Nikoloz Samkharadze, who chairs parliament’s Foreign Relations Committee, also studied in Germany on a Konrad Adenauer Foundation scholarship. In 2003, the foundation funded his master’s degree in European studies at the University of Hanover.
For Tina Khidasheli, the Georgian government members’ ties to Germany are the main reason for the current problems.
“[Georgian Dream founder] Bidzina Ivanishvili demanded that they ‘sort things out’ with Germany, but they failed to do so. This subsequently gave way to aggressive rhetoric,” Khidasheli believes.

articles.title: Zelensky: Ukraine is ready to freeze the conflict along the front line and start negotiations with Russia - Gazeta Express
articles.summary: Zelensky: Ukraine is ready to freeze the conflict along the front line and start negotiations with Russia  Gazeta Express
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared on Wednesday that Ukraine is ready to freeze the conflict along the current front line and move towards diplomatic negotiations, as part of efforts to end the war with Russia.
In an interview with American television Fox News, Zelenskyy said that Kiev then intends to seek security guarantees from the United States and European countries.
"Yes. For now we need to freeze the conflict and I think this is a real way to end this war," he said, adding that a ceasefire is the minimum that Ukraine expects from Russia.
He said that Kiev would then turn to the US president and European leaders to seek security guarantees, stressing that peace and security are the most important priorities.
Asked whether Ukraine would agree to give up the Donbas region in exchange for an end to the war, Zelenskyy rejected the claim that Russia is winning on the battlefield. According to him, Moscow is trying to pressure Kiev to withdraw from its territories.
"In 2026, they have not succeeded. They are not winning on the battlefield," he claimed.
Zelenskyy acknowledged that Ukrainians are tired of war, but stressed that the country cannot simply give up its territories.
He reiterated that negotiations should start from current positions on the battlefield, while a peace plan should be drawn up through diplomacy.
The Ukrainian president also described as "productive" the previous day's meeting in Oslo, Norway, with US special envoy Steve Witkoff.
He thanked the Norwegian prime minister for organizing the talks, which were also attended by European leaders and US officials, including Jared Kushner, who joined remotely.
Zelenskyy said the discussions focused on possible steps towards peace and expressed hope that Witkoff's meeting in Russia would bring an answer.
According to him, possible first steps to reduce tensions could include ceasefires covering food security, maritime activities and energy infrastructure.
Zelenskyy said he immediately supported the idea of a ceasefire in the energy sector, proposed by US President Donald Trump.
"I hope that today, within a few hours, we will have some results," he added.

articles.title: Putin orders release of jailed American as he meets Trump envoy for Ukraine talks | Russia - The Guardian
articles.summary: Putin orders release of jailed American as he meets Trump envoy for Ukraine talks | Russia  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
Vladimir Putin ordered the release of an American man from a Russian jail as he met Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on Wednesday for fresh talks on ending the war in Ukraine, amid increasingly close relations between Moscow and Washington.
Trump had previously asked Putin to free Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher who had spent more than four years in Russian jails on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine.
His release appeared to be Moscow’s latest calculated move to bring Trump further into line with Putin’s position on Ukraine, while offering the US president a diplomatic victory before the midterm elections.
Hubbard was released unilaterally by Russia, rather than as part of a prisoner exchange as has often been the case with previous releases of Americans held in the country.
Writing on social media after the release was announced, Trump said it followed a request he had made “directly” to Putin last week.
He wrote on Truth Social: “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia … There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release.”
Hubbard’s younger sister told the Associated Press she had spoken to her brother, who said he had thought he was “going to die in prison”.
“He’s out of Russia territory. He is free, praise God,” Patricia Hubbard Fox said, adding that her brother suffered beatings and starvation while he was held captive.
Witkoff, meanwhile, lavished praise on Putin during their meeting at the grand Constantine Palace in St Petersburg, describing the Russian president as a humanitarian.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff told Putin. He also conveyed Trump’s thanks for a deal to resume Russian diesel exports to the US.
The Russian president is wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) as a war criminal, in relation to the deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia during the war.
More than 17,500 civilians have been confirmed killed in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the UN, which says the true toll is likely to be significantly higher.
The warmth of Witkoff’s remarks stood in stark contrast to the increasingly hostile rhetoric directed at Volodymyr Zelenskyy by senior US officials, most notably Trump, who has called for the Ukrainian president to resign and portrayed him as the main obstacle to peace.
Witkoff travelled to Russia from Oslo, where he had met Zelenskyy and European leaders a day earlier in an attempt to inject momentum into stalled negotiations, with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year.
Witkoff told Putin during a televised portion of their meeting: “We’ve brought some papers. It’s really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you’ll read that at your leisure.”
The visit was Witkoff’s ninth to Russia since Trump tasked him with brokering an end to the war.
Witkoff described his meeting with Putin as “constructive” but said “important work” remained and trilateral talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine “at the technical level” would follow.
The Kremlin said it had agreed “in principle” to the talks, which would focus on how to guarantee the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war ended.
The latest rupture in relations between Washington and Kyiv was triggered by Trump’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal with Putin, followed by his call for Zelenskyy to be replaced after Ukraine refused to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Kyiv has since complained of disruptions to US intelligence-sharing and restrictions on its access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network.
Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that Washington had resumed providing advance warnings of Russian missile attacks after his meeting with Witkoff in Oslo.
But Ukraine continues to face restrictions on Starshield, although it remains unclear who ordered them. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had personally ordered the slowdown, while Reuters, citing sources, said the directive had come from inside the White House.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said on Wednesday that the decision to restrict Ukraine’s access came from Musk.
“I’m not aware that we knew about this decision beforehand. But that’s irrelevant,” Rubio told reporters during a trip to India.
“The bottom line is that, that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at.”
During Wednesday’s meeting with Witkoff, Putin thanked Trump and his wife, Melania, for “their attention to efforts to end the war”.
Yet there are few signs of an imminent breakthrough. Despite repeated Ukrainian calls for a ceasefire, including a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, Moscow has given little indication that it intends to end its bombardment of Ukraine as winter approaches, apparently confident that continued pressure will help it extract greater concessions from Kyiv.
The Russian leader remains intent on sticking to his maximalist war aims, including his demand for full Russian control of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region.
Putin also sought to emphasise the prospects for closer economic ties between Russia and the US once the war ends, suggesting that Moscow could significantly increase its exports of fertilisers to the American market.
Russian officials said the first tanker carrying diesel to the US would depart on Thursday as part of an initial shipment of about 300,000 tonnes.
Energy analysts and traders have questioned whether Trump’s agreement to temporarily resume Russian diesel imports will deliver meaningful relief to US consumers before the midterm elections, arguing that the volumes involved are too small to significantly ease the global supply squeeze.
The talks on Wednesday also touched on a possible meeting in China next month between Putin, Trump and the Chinese president, Xi Jinping. The Kremlin said Beijing was already making preparations for what it described as an unprecedented summit between the three leaders.

articles.title: Hong Kong seeks bigger role in Belt and Road financial cooperation: InvestHK official - Global Times
articles.summary: Hong Kong seeks bigger role in Belt and Road financial cooperation: InvestHK official  Global Times
articles.full_text:
Photo taken on October 20, 2026 shows the landscape design of the Annual Conference of Financial Street Forum 2026 in Beijing. Photo: Yin Yeping/Global Times
Hong Kong is looking to help Belt and Road countries access offshore yuan bonds and loans to lower borrowing costs and support infrastructure development, while connecting the Chinese mainland financial institutions and technology providers with overseas markets, Associate Director-General of Investment Promotion at Invest Hong Kong King Leung told the Global Times in an exclusive interview at the Annual Conference of Financial Street Forum 2026 in Beijing.
Leung said some Central Asian countries face particularly high borrowing costs, with local business leaders telling Hong Kong representatives that interest rates in their markets could reach 25 percent.
"By having yuan bonds, this can drastically lower the cost of borrowing, or cost of capital," Leung said, adding that offshore yuan financing and loans could help accelerate infrastructure development in these countries.
Such financing could support projects including off-grid power solutions using solar and wind energy combined with energy storage, he said, noting that mainland companies with advanced technological capabilities could establish their international headquarters in Hong Kong to manage their global expansion and provide solutions tailored to local needs.
Hong Kong has a dedicated Belt and Road Office to help establish connections with countries participating in the initiative. In recent months, the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) government has stepped up engagement with emerging markets, including Central Asian countries such as Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, Leung said.
The HKSAR Chief Executive John Lee also led a delegation to Central Asia in recent months to explore cooperation opportunities, he noted.
Meanwhile, Hong Kong representatives led delegations to Southeast Asia and Gulf Cooperation Council countries, with commercial discussions already underway. While not all these discussions involve governments, Leung said the outreach had gained good traction, with local partners welcoming Chinese technology and capital.
The approach reflects Hong Kong's role in connecting the mainland with international markets, while leveraging its own financial strengths under the principle of "one country, two systems," Leung said.
Hong Kong's financial development should align with the national agenda, including the latest 15th Five Year Plan, while taking advantage of its distinctive regulatory arrangements and close links with international markets, he said.
One area where Hong Kong can contribute is digital assets. Leung described the city as a "sandbox" for experimenting with different applications of digital assets, citing its regulatory independence under the "one country, two systems" framework.
He said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority had issued two licenses this year to firms seeking to issue stablecoins, including one backed by Standard Chartered Bank and another by HSBC.
Although stablecoins are not permitted on the Chinese mainland, Leung noted that different forms of digital money were being explored, including the digital yuan, or e-CNY, and tokenized deposits.
Hong Kong's experience with tokenized green bonds also offers opportunities for international cooperation, particularly in emerging markets seeking to advance their green transitions.
Leung said Hong Kong had been a pioneer in issuing tokenized green bonds, with the first such government issuance taking place in 2023. Distributed ledger technology, including blockchain, can improve data tracking and transparency, helping monitor the use of funds and identify potential greenwashing, he said.
Such initiatives are particularly relevant to developing economies, where financial innovation can help mobilize funding for sustainable development, he said.
Leung, who oversees financial services related to investment promotion at Invest Hong Kong, said he attended the Financial Street Forum for the first time this year to meet financial leaders and gain a better understanding of the direction of financial sector development on the mainland.
Associate Director-General of Investment Promotion at Invest Hong Kong King Leung attends the Financial Street Forum in Beijing on October 20, 2026. Photo: Yin Yeping/Global Times
He highlighted the forum's discussions on green finance, financial innovation and digital green bonds as a mechanism for promoting the green transition, particularly in Global South countries.
Beyond financing, fintech offers another avenue for cooperation with emerging markets, Leung said.
The InvestHK official said business leaders and sovereign wealth funds in these markets consistently identified fintech as one of the leading emerging sectors receiving government attention, and many also cited Chinese experience in promoting financial inclusion.
Leung pointed to Shenzhen based digital bank WeBank, which uses technology to serve customers who might not previously have had bank accounts and provide small loans. WeBank has established a fintech unit in Hong Kong in recent years to export its technological capabilities to other emerging markets.
Leung described Hong Kong's role as a bridge for mainland fintech companies seeking international opportunities.
Hong Kong's approach was to understand the needs of emerging markets and help provide both capital and technological expertise through cooperation with overseas financial institutions and mainland companies, said Leung.
"It's a win-win situation for all," Leung said.

articles.full_text:
New agreement with Uzbekistan Technological Metals Complex and the Uzbekistan Fund for Reconstruction and Development advances collaboration beyond the November 2025 MOU toward a commercial demonstration program
Following successful technical validation of Uzbek-sourced tungsten, ReElement will advance commercial demonstration activities and evaluate future deployment of its advanced refining technology in Uzbekistan
Collaboration establishes a new model for U.S.-Uzbekistan critical mineral cooperation focused on domestic value creation, technology deployment, and mutually beneficial supply chains
FISHERS, IN / ACCESS Newswire / October 21, 2026 / American Resources Corporation AREC ("American Resources" or "AREC"), together with ReElement Technologies Corporation ("ReElement"), a leading U.S. developer and operator of advanced critical mineral separation and refining technologies in which American Resources maintains a strategic minority interest, today announced the execution of a new agreement with Uzbekistan Technological Metals Complex ("UzTMK") and the Fund for Reconstruction and Development of the Republic of Uzbekistan ("UFRD") to advance their strategic collaboration in tungsten processing and refining.
The agreement was signed on October 19, 2026, in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, during the American-Uzbek Business and Investment Council event, held in connection with broader U.S.-Uzbekistan and C5+1 diplomatic and commercial engagements involving President Shavkat Mirziyoyev of Uzbekistan, Saida Mirziyoyeva, Head of the Presidential Administration of Uzbekistan, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and U.S. Special Envoy for South and Central Asian Affairs Sergio Gor. The signing reflects the growing commitment of both countries to strengthen bilateral economic cooperation, expand investment, and develop more secure and diversified critical mineral supply chains.
The new agreement advances the parties' November 2025 memorandum of understanding beyond initial technical evaluation toward a structured commercial demonstration and engineering program. Through the existing collaboration, ReElement has successfully validated the processing of Uzbek-sourced tungsten into high-purity oxide form using its proprietary refining technology.
Tungsten is an increasingly strategic critical mineral essential to industrial, defense, aerospace, advanced manufacturing, and electronics applications. With global tungsten supply chains highly concentrated and increasingly subject to geopolitical and trade-related disruptions, secure, diversified refining capacity has become a growing priority. ReElement's proprietary, modular refining platform is designed around a demand-aligned refining model, producing high-purity critical mineral products tailored to downstream customer specifications while aligning processing capacity with commercial demand.
Under the newly executed agreement, the parties have agreed on expanded technological evaluation and a commercial demonstration program utilizing Uzbek-sourced tungsten at ReElement's U.S. facilities, designed to further validate commercial viability, processing efficiencies, product quality, and scalability.
An equally important component of the collaboration is the advancement of preliminary engineering, process design, and techno-economic modeling for potential tungsten refining operations in Uzbekistan, as the parties evaluate opportunities to establish higher-value processing and refining capabilities closer to the source of the minerals.
The agreement also establishes a joint working group of all four parties to coordinate technical activities, engineering and economic evaluations, and subsequent project proposals, and includes opportunities for Uzbek technical specialists to visit ReElement's U.S. facilities and evaluate additional applications of the technology.
The initiative reflects a new model for international critical mineral development - one that moves beyond the traditional approach of extracting, concentrating, and exporting raw materials. Instead, the parties are connecting complementary capabilities across resource development, advanced processing, refining, and downstream industrial markets to maximize economic benefits for both countries.
For Uzbekistan, this approach has the potential to support domestic industrial development, technological advancement, skilled employment, and greater value creation from its mineral resources. For the United States, it offers expanded access to diversified critical mineral supplies while supporting American-developed refining technologies.
Mark Jensen, Chairman and CEO of American Resources Corporation and ReElement Technologies, commented: "We are extremely pleased to advance our relationship with UzTMK and UFRD beyond the MOU stage and into a clearly defined commercial demonstration program. Our initial success in refining Uzbek-sourced tungsten provides an important technical foundation for this next phase.
"We believe we have reached a pivotal moment when mineral security has never been more important to economic prosperity and national security. Cooperation between the United States and Uzbekistan can establish a new model for critical mineral supply chains - one built on collaboration and mutual economic benefit. We believe Uzbekistan is the ideal country to pioneer this model of cooperation. Our objective is not simply to move raw materials from one country to another, but to deploy technology that creates higher-value products for both countries."
American Resources and ReElement believe this collaboration is a practical example of how American innovation and Uzbekistan's resource and industrial strengths can be de-risked and connected to deliver lasting economic value to both nations.

articles.title: Rubio Gets a Medal. Russia Gets Military Drills. Karakalpakstan Gets Silence. - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
articles.summary: Rubio Gets a Medal. Russia Gets Military Drills. Karakalpakstan Gets Silence.  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

source_detail.name: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

articles.full_text:
On October 19, Uzbekistan’s President Shavkat Mirziyoyev awarded U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio the Order of Outstanding Merit. On October 20, UzDaily reported the arrival of Russian troops for joint military exercises in Uzbekistan. For Karakalpak families awaiting the release of political prisoners, neither announcement offered relief. Uzbekistan celebrated American investment and welcomed Russian soldiers while making no publicly announced commitment to people imprisoned for exercising and defending their rights.
Mirziyoyev’s office announced $12 billion in agreements, while Rubio participated in the C5+1 ministerial meeting and witnessed Uzbekistan’s signing of the Artemis Accords on peaceful space exploration. Sustained American engagement with Central Asia serves legitimate interests, and investment can create opportunities across the region. But announced agreements must still become functioning projects.
The more immediate political benefit went to Mirziyoyev, who received the public appreciation of America’s top diplomat. Rubio wrote that he was “deeply honored to be awarded the Order of Outstanding Merit by President Mirziyoyev” on X. The public results of the visit offered no hint of discussion on Karakalpak prisoners or accountability for the July 2022 massacre in Karakalpakstan.
The Russian exercises make it harder to mistake American access for a strategic shift in Tashkent. According to UzDaily, citing Russia’s Central Military District, servicemen from the 201st Guards Military Base – a Russian base in Tajikistan – arrived for Hamkorlik-2026, scheduled for October 20-27 in Uzbekistan. The report described the participation of assault units, reconnaissance and strike drones, robotic systems, and Mi-24 helicopters. These drills need not have been organized as a message to Washington to illustrate Tashkent’s position. Uzbekistan could welcome an American secretary of state and Russian military personnel in the same week without treating either relationship as a concession to the other.
Mirziyoyev had already explained that position in his own words. During an October 7 birthday call with Putin, he praised the Russian president’s “historic role” in modern Russia and his contribution to their countries’ “comprehensive strategic partnership and alliance.” That same day, he received a delegation led by Denis Manturov to advance cooperation in industry, energy, metallurgy, nuclear energy, and industrial zones. Earlier, Putin had authorized negotiations to amend military-technical agreements with Uzbekistan. RFE/RL reported in August that the proposed changes remained undisclosed.
Uzbekistan has been equally adept at cultivating other partners. Mirziyoyev signed the charter of President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace in January. His Interior Ministry has described cooperation with Huawei, including plans for “intelligent video surveillance.” In September, an institute under the Agriculture Ministry announced a memorandum with Iran’s Sirang UAV covering agricultural drone training and service centers. That agreement concerns agricultural applications and does not establish military cooperation or imply sanctions evasion, but it does illustrate a developing relationship. Washington should judge its own successes by the commitments it obtains, rather than assume that a warm reception will translate into influence.
The commercial relationship requires the same scrutiny. In April, the EU imposed sanctions on Uzbek companies over their Russia links, citing cotton-cellulose supplies to Russian gunpowder manufacturers. Those findings give U.S. officials concrete reasons to insist on rigorous screening of counterparties, beneficial ownership, and supply chains before promoting investment. Uzbekistan’s political system presents additional concerns: Freedom House rates it “Not Free,” with a score of 12 out of 100, while the Human Rights Foundation classifies it as a fully authoritarian regime. Freedom House reports that no opposition parties operate legally and that the legislature and judiciary effectively serve the executive.
American investors have encountered the consequences of weak institutional protections before. In 2006, Newmont disclosed approximately $48 million in tax claims against its Uzbek joint venture despite written confirmation from Uzbekistan’s Justice Ministry that a relevant tax decree applied for the venture’s lifetime. Access to the venture’s bank accounts was restricted, its assets placed under legal restraint, and bankruptcy proceedings initiated. A 2007 settlement provided for $80 million in payments and the transfer of Newmont’s interest to Uzbek parties, without an admission of liability. These events occurred when Shavkat Mirziyoyev was Uzbekistan’s prime minister.
The OECD’s 2025 investment review identifies continuing concerns about executive influence over courts, inconsistent decisions in technically complex cases, and overlapping rules that undermine predictability. Investors therefore have reason to ask whether commitments will survive a change of leadership, a reshuffle of influential officials, or a dispute involving politically connected interests. Official assurances offer limited protection unless institutions can enforce them.
The U.S. also has a strategic lesson to remember. After the May 2005 Andijan crackdown, the United States supported calls for an independent international investigation. That July, Uzbekistan ordered American forces out of the Karshi-Khanabad airbase, which supported operations in Afghanistan. Years of security cooperation failed to preserve American access once accountability became a source of bilateral tension. If Washington now avoids difficult questions to protect its agreements, Tashkent again holds considerable leverage over the relationship.
For Karakalpak people, those questions are urgent. Dauletmurat Tajimuratov, a Karakalpak lawyer and journalist, received a 16-year sentence after opposing proposed constitutional changes affecting the Sovereign Republic of Karakalpakstan’s status. The United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found his imprisonment arbitrary and called for his immediate release. Another two and a half years were added to his sentence this year. Before Rubio’s visit, Kaitie Holland and Sergei Korotkov, both international legal associates at the Human Rights Foundation, urged him in an article published by Just Security to demand freedom for Uzbekistan’s political prisoners, detailing Tajimuratov’s reported beatings, degrading prison conditions, and attempts to force him to renounce his Karakalpak identity.
In June, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer reaffirmed strong support for Uzbekistan’s World Trade Organization (WTO) accession. Further discretionary benefits should accompany published commitments on prisoner protection, accountability, and predictable legal treatment. Washington should press for Tajimuratov’s release, independent medical and monitoring access pending release, and an independent international investigation into the 2022 massacre. Independent courts and limits on executive interference would also protect the American businesses the administration is encouraging to invest.
Tashkent played its hand well. Mirziyoyev secured American recognition and commercial support while strengthening ties with Russia and maintaining an iron grip at home. Rubio must now explain what Washington obtained in return. Until commercial promises become enforceable commitments and American influence helps secure freedom for political prisoners, the medal around Rubio’s neck offers clearer evidence of Mirziyoyev’s diplomatic success than America’s.

articles.title: Uzbekistan promises US businesses “clear and predictable conditions” - Газета.uz
articles.summary: Uzbekistan promises US businesses “clear and predictable conditions”  Газета.uz
articles.full_text:
Relations between Uzbekistan and the United States have reached their “highest level” in the history of bilateral cooperation, president Shavkat Mirziyoyev said at the second meeting of the US-Uzbekistan Business and Investment Council in Samarkand on 19 October. He highlighted the role of US president Donald Trump in developing ties.
“We have established a strong political partnership. It is now important to expand our economic ties as well,” the president said.
He noted that hundreds of companies with US capital operate in Uzbekistan, while Uzbek companies are beginning to invest in the US economy. “We want companies from both countries to establish more joint ventures, exchange technologies and enter new markets together,” Mirziyoyev said.
“We need to create clear and predictable conditions for American investors”
The president identified critical minerals, energy, digital technologies and artificial intelligence as promising areas for cooperation.
“Uzbekistan has substantial natural resources and is ready to become a reliable partner of the United States in this field. It is important for us to develop the entire production cycle, from developing deposits and advanced processing of raw materials to manufacturing finished high-technology products,” he said.
“Our rapidly growing economy needs a modern and reliable energy system. We invite American companies to participate in its modernization, introduce new technologies and develop renewable energy and energy storage systems,” he added.
The president proposed taking the two countries' partnership in digital technologies and artificial intelligence to a “new level”.
“We see considerable opportunities for cooperation in establishing data centers and applying the most effective digital solutions in industry, agriculture, education and public administration,” he said.
Mirziyoyev noted that Uzbekistan and the United States had put together a package of 54 agreements and initiatives worth around $12 billion as part of the meeting. To implement these projects, he proposed developing an action plan focused on three priorities.
“First, we need to create clear and predictable conditions for American investors. Every company coming to Uzbekistan with serious intentions should know who to contact and a way to obtain their assistance it needs,” Mirziyoyev said.
He said Uzbekistan intended to adopt a new model for working with foreign investors based on the “Plant and Play” principle.
“We offer modern investment opportunities. We offer fully prepared projects with ready-to-use sites, infrastructure connections and all necessary permits and documentation,” the president said, adding that Uzbek entrepreneurs were ready to act as partners and share investment risks.
A direct investment fund has been established to support participation in such projects.
“Our task is to ensure that an American investor arriving in Uzbekistan can begin doing business immediately without spending time on administrative procedures,” the president said.
The second area, according to Mirziyoyev, should focus on moving from individual projects to broad industrial partnerships, establishing joint clusters and research centers and integrating companies from both countries into global value chains.
As the third area, the president proposed turning the council into a “strategic mechanism for a long-term economic partnership” between the two countries.
“I propose developing a joint program for trade, investment and technological cooperation for the period through 2035. This program will align the interests of major companies with the strategic priorities of our countries,” he said.
“The national interests of the US and Uzbekistan align”
US secretary of state Marco Rubio, who visited Samarkand with a large business delegation, said Washington viewed relations with Central Asia as a priority and wanted to strengthen its partnership with both the region as a whole and Uzbekistan in particular.
“Let there be no doubt that the United States wants to be a partner of this region and wants to be a partner of this country. We already are, and we intend to build that and grow it,” Rubio said.
He said the US had long focused on problem regions, countries or issues, overlooking new opportunities.
“One of the regions of the world we should have been involved in sooner and in a bigger way is Central Asia, and in particular Uzbekistan,” the secretary of state said.
He stated that Trump had made developing relations with Central Asia one of the US priorities. Rubio also described the invitation extended to several Central Asian countries, including Uzbekistan, to attend the G20 summit in Miami, US, as observers at the end of the year as an important step.
The secretary of state linked the development of bilateral relations to Uzbekistan’s reforms in recent years.
“You have opened up your country to the world, and more importantly, you have embraced the United States and president Trump as partners. And as a result, you’ve given not just to your country but the region — your neighbors — as well as the United States, an enormous opportunity to grow together,” he said, addressing Mirziyoyev.
Rubio also expressed his appreciation to the co-chairs of the US-Uzbekistan Business and Investment Council: head of the Presidential Administration of Uzbekistan Saida Mirziyoyeva and the US president’s special envoy Sergio Gor.
“We just call her Saida because we see her in so many different places, and she’s so talented and so smart and works so hard,” he said.
Rubio stressed that cooperation was based on the alignment of the two countries' national interests.
“When your national interests and our national interests are aligned — and they are, in so many areas — when what’s good for America is also good for you and vice versa, that is the foundation of these partnerships and these opportunities that we are pursuing. And that’s what this is all about, and that’s what we’re doing now as regards to this,” he said.
According to the secretary of state, Central Asia’s geographical location offers additional opportunities.
“Uzbekistan, and Central Asia more broadly, have always been the center of commerce and transit between the East and the West. It has literally been the bridge between East and West when it came to trade and commerce. It has been true for centuries. And geography has not changed. It remains more true today than ever before,” Rubio said.
He noted the growth of passenger and freight transport in Uzbekistan, as well as the country’s potential in technology and infrastructure. Rubio cited Uzbekistan’s central location for trade, its large working-age population and its natural resources among the factors that make the country attractive to American businesses.
Rubio added that the US and Uzbekistan could also develop cooperation in energy, robotics, fintech, mining and agriculture.
“I'm extremely optimistic about the future of business and growth in Central Asia. We are doing our part to lay the regulatory and commercial foundation upon which your businesses will power and grow,” the secretary of state said, addressing the meeting’s participants.
“Business moves where rules are clear”
Head of Uzbekistan’s Presidential Administration Saida Mirziyoyeva said the US-Uzbekistan Business and Investment Council would serve as a working mechanism for resolving business problems.
“We promise your side a working mechanism, not a committee. In June, almost 200 American companies came to Tashkent — a record. Four months later, another hundred US companies came with the secretary. Records in this partnership do not last long, and we like it that way,” she said.
Mirziyoyeva noted that clear rules and openness were essential for business development.
“Business moves where rules are clear, doors are open and someone picks up the phone,” she said.
“When business asked, we changed the rules, and now the trade runs both ways. Uzbek investment is creating jobs in America, and what we buy from America keeps American factories busy. That is how a partnership stays honest. Both sides have to win,” the head of the Presidential Administration said.
“And so tonight, a simple promise: Every company here will have a name to call, and any problem you raise will reach the co-chairs personally,” Mirziyoyeva added.
The head of the Presidential Administration also backed the repeal of the Jackson-Vanik amendment, which the US secretary of state called a “relic of the Cold War”.
“We agree and we would be happy to see it retire. When it does, this council will be ready the next morning,” she said.
In closing, Mirziyoyeva urged businesses to move from discussing potential to taking concrete action. “Bring us a project or bring us a problem. Both are welcome,” she said.

articles.title: US and Central Asian Countries Outline Shared Vision in Joint Statement at C5+1 Meeting - The Astana Times
articles.summary: US and Central Asian Countries Outline Shared Vision in Joint Statement at C5+1 Meeting  The Astana Times
articles.full_text:
ASTANA – The United States and five Central Asian countries reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening economic, energy, security, and cultural cooperation at the C5+1 Ministerial meeting in Samarkand on Oct. 19.
In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan, and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio shared a vision for an enduring U.S.-Central Asian partnership, grounded in respect for sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity, reported the U.S. Department of State on Oct. 19.
As the Central Asian countries celebrate 35 years of independence and the United States marks 250 years of independence, the governments expressed their commitment to a more peaceful, prosperous future.
“We envision the United States and Central Asia as enduring partners of choice,” the statement said.
The countries pledged to strengthen transportation links, invest in infrastructure along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, and forge digital connections, including through English-language training and education.
They also committed to developing regional economic integration through expanded intraregional trade, improved transport connectivity, harmonized customs procedures, and stronger industrial cooperation.
The statement highlighted opportunities to increase two-way trade and investment, expand e-commerce, and create commercial opportunities for American companies in Central Asia and Central Asian enterprises in the U.S. market.
The countries identified energy cooperation and critical minerals as key priorities, aiming to develop integrated, high-value supply chains, expand mineral extraction and processing, and increase production of value-added goods for international markets.
The governments also pledged to strengthen security cooperation, notably in countering terrorism and transnational organized crime, enhancing border security, and addressing human trafficking, illicit drug trafficking, arms trafficking, and cybercrime.
They reaffirmed their commitment to nuclear security, safeguards, the physical protection of nuclear material, and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.
The statement also emphasized preserving cultural heritage and expanding professional, cultural, and educational exchanges.
Speaking at the meeting, Rubio described Central Asia as a historic crossroads for East-West trade and an increasingly important destination for investment and exports.
“The C5+1 represents not only America’s interest in – but America’s commitment to – fostering closer, peaceful relations with Central Asian countries,” Rubio said.
He noted that the previous C5+1 meeting in Washington had yielded $25 billion in new deals across transportation, energy, finance, and other sectors.
“This group has an opportunity to partner and radically grow our countries in ways unseen in recent history,” he said.
Uzbekistan Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov said the partnership’s next stage should focus on strengthening economic connectivity, attracting advanced technologies and investment, and expanding access to global markets.
He also proposed advancing a strategic partnership in critical minerals, from geological exploration and mineral processing to the establishment of local industrial clusters.
Saidov said Uzbekistan, assuming the C5+1 Secretariat’s co-chairmanship, intends to build on previous achievements and focus on turning agreements into practical results.

articles.title: Russia willing to resume trilateral peace talks in November, Kremlin says after Witkoff meeting - CNN
articles.summary: Russia willing to resume trilateral peace talks in November, Kremlin says after Witkoff meeting  CNN
articles.full_text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin said the Kremlin would be ready to resume trilateral Russia-US-Ukraine peace talks after mid-November, at the request of US special envoy Steve Witkoff who met with Putin for around three hours Wednesday.
The meeting in St. Petersburg came off the back of Witkoff’s “productive” Tuesday summit with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Norway, as the United States seeks to advance proposals to end to the war.
Putin said he would be ready to resume trilateral talks after November 10, according to a post-meeting briefing by his aide Yury Ushakov. The aide said the Kremlin would like to discuss the establishment of a “security framework” for both Russia and Ukraine following the end of the conflict, without offering further details on what Russia would demand as part of that framework.
The next trilateral round could take place in Abu Dhabi, the capital city of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Ushakov said in response to a question on Russian state news channel Russia 24.
Zelensky said on Wednesday that he would like the meeting to happen “no later than the beginning of November.”
“Russia said many times it is ready for a meeting and then things changed and got cancelled,” Zelensky added. “Let’s see what happens this time.”
A readout from a US official confirmed that the meeting took place, adding that it was aimed at advancing US President Donald Trump’s efforts to end Russia’s war with Ukraine.
Witkoff described the meetings both with Putin and Zelensky as “constructive” in a post on X after the meeting Wednesday, and said the discussions would continue with the trilateral talks.
“While there is still important work left to do, President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end and achieving a comprehensive, durable peace,” he wrote.
US envoys Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner proposed a trilateral meeting which was “accepted by the Ukrainians in Oslo yesterday and by the Russians in St. Petersburg today,” the readout said.
Despite the positive comments on potential future negotiations, there are no indications so far that Russia has budged on any of its maximalist positions.
Russia’s previous demands amount to near-total victory – calling for Ukraine to give up the entire eastern Ukrainian Donbas region, which is now mostly under Russian occupation. Moscow has also called for Ukraine to dramatically reduce the size of its military and pledge to never join NATO.
During the latest talks, Putin expressed interest in the topic of restoring economic cooperation with the United States and the possibility of a meeting with China to discuss Ukraine. That follows recent moves by the Trump administration to waive sanctions on Russia and strike a deal on diesel exports.
Speaking to media after the meeting, Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev said there was “no question” that US-Russian economic cooperation would continue, and added that a recently-announced diesel deal between the two countries would go ahead despite European criticism.
A key outcome of the meeting was Witkoff announcing that Russia has released 74-year-old American prisoner Stephen Hubbard, who has been detained in the country for more than four years. A video obtained by CNN after the meeting shows Hubbard speaking with Witkoff at the airport in St. Petersburg.
In video of the beginning of the three-hour meeting, Witkoff said, “I think there’s some degree of momentum, and I hope that this today can be another step forward in the peace process.”
Putin, Witkoff and translators sat around a large round table as they also discussed a wide range of issues including Russia’s willingness to help resolve the war in Iran, potential Russian fertilizer exports to the US and the release of Hubbard. The meeting continued behind closed doors, and Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law who has also been involved in the peace negotiations, joined remotely given he has the flu.
The US and Ukraine made “meaningful progress” in the Norway talks on Tuesday, a US official previously told CNN. Ukraine “brought forward new ideas and proposals, which were discussed in detail,” and the two sides are now in “strong alignment” on what the next steps will be, the official said.
“Discussions covered key elements of a comprehensive peace framework, including long-term security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic and prosperity plan, and a broader European security architecture designed to create lasting stability,” the US official said.
But Kremlin aide Ushakov poured cold water on those discussions on Wednesday, saying that while Witkoff had highlighted to Putin “certain new approaches and developments in the positions taken by the Europeans and Kyiv… in truth, these contained little of actual value for resolving the Ukrainian crisis.”
Ukraine and its allies have reiterated the key red lines set by Kyiv for any peace negotiations, including the need for future security guarantees – to ensure Russia doesn’t invade again – and a rejection of any demands to give up territory it controls.
“Much depends on whether the American side will hear something new from Russia today – about peace, rather than the continuation of the war,” Zelensky said on Wednesday, following another meeting with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre.
Zelensky repeated a long-held position that Ukraine would accept a ceasefire deal that involves a freeze along the current frontline – something that would involve retaining only about 75% of Ukrainian land – and would then ask allies for meaningful security guarantees.
“Right now we have to freeze, and I think this is (the) real way to end this war,” the Ukrainian president told Fox News on Wednesday. “This is (the) minimum of what we need from Russia today. Then of course we’ll go to the president and to Europeans and we’ll ask (for) security guarantees.”
Zelensky also said that Ukraine also wants trilateral negotiations involving Trump, Putin and himself, but the process would be “better with Europeans.”
“I always said that we are open to negotiate in any format, any topics, but don’t speak about us without us, please,” he said, balking at the prospect of any Russia-China-US negotiations.
The Kremlin has previously shut down the idea of trilateral negotiations, apart from a previous invitation for Zelensky to come to Moscow – something viewed as unviable by the other sides.
Regarding the Norway talks with the Ukrainian side, the US official added: “The teams are working exceptionally well together, with a shared commitment to finding practical solutions to end the war,” striking a positive tone despite the souring public relationship between Zelensky and Trump.
“The goal is to build on the progress made with Ukraine and Europe, discuss the proposals with Russia, and create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations,” the US official said.
Meanwhile in Russia, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on Tuesday struck a less upbeat tone, saying that Moscow will see what Witkoff brings to the table but will not make “political concessions.” Lavrov said that Moscow does “not expect a miracle” and Washington will remain a rival to Russia “at best,” according to Russian state media TASS.
A European official in Oslo told CNN: “I think plans – or lack of – isn’t as much of a problem as getting Russia to treat any plan seriously.”
This is a developing story and will be updated.
CNN’s Ivana Kottasová, Kevin Liptak, Nick Paton Walsh and Kosta Gak contributed to this report.

articles.title: The Republic Of Kazakhstan: From The Declaration Of State Sovereignty To Middle-Power Status In 36 Years - Analysis - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: The Republic Of Kazakhstan: From The Declaration Of State Sovereignty To Middle-Power Status In 36 Years - Analysis  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- On 25 October 1990, Kazakhstan adopted the Declaration of State Sovereignty, establishing principles of autonomy, territorial integrity, and independent international relations that preceded formal independence on 16 December 1991 and continue to guide its multi-vector foreign policy.
- The economy has expanded from resource dependence toward diversification, with 2025 GDP at 159.6 trillion tenge (about US$306 billion, real growth 6.5 percent), plans to attract US$150 billion in foreign investment by 2029, and rising rankings in innovation and e-government indices, while transit corridors such as the Middle Corridor are being developed.
- Marking 34 years of diplomatic relations with Slovenia, Kazakhstan highlights growing trade (reaching €193.5 million in 2025) and potential cooperation in pharmaceuticals, digital technology, logistics, and infrastructure as part of broader European engagement.
On 25 October, Kazakhstan celebrates Republic Day, a national holiday of particular historical significance for the formation of modern Kazakh statehood. On this day in 1990, the Declaration of State Sovereignty of the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic was adopted, marking a major political and legal milestone on the path to independence. Thirty-six years later, the principles set out in the Declaration—sovereignty, territorial integrity, autonomy and responsibility for the country’s own future—continue to shape Kazakhstan’s strategic development.
For Kazakhstan, the date is not only an opportunity to look back at the origins of modern statehood, but also to reflect on the journey so far, assess the results achieved and identify priorities for further development. At a time of profound change in international relations, accelerating technological advances and growing interdependence among states, a country’s ability to set its own national priorities, modernise its economy consistently and strengthen the confidence of international partners takes on particular importance.
Historical Choices and the Formation of Statehood
Adopted on 25 October 1990, the Declaration of State Sovereignty was one of the key documents that established the political and legal foundations of Kazakhstan’s future independence. It enshrined the principles of autonomy for the republican authorities, territorial integrity, citizenship, economic independence and the right to conduct independent international relations. The document thus marked a transition to a new understanding of the state’s responsibility to its people and laid the groundwork for the subsequent formation of the independent Republic of Kazakhstan.
The proclamation of state independence on 16 December 1991 was a natural continuation of this historical process. The country faced enormous tasks: establishing independent state institutions, creating a national legal system, transitioning to a market economy, building foreign-policy ties and integrating into the international community. These processes unfolded in difficult economic and geopolitical conditions, requiring both strategic vision and the ability to make complex practical decisions.
In the first years of independence, Kazakhstan established the fundamental principles of its statehood: preserving territorial integrity, strengthening interethnic harmony, developing national culture, maintaining domestic stability and pursuing an independent foreign policy. The multinational character of society became not an obstacle but an important factor in shaping a model of statehood in which civic identity is combined with respect for cultural and linguistic diversity.
Building its own system of international relations was of vital importance. Kazakhstan established diplomatic ties with countries around the world, joined international organisations and treaties, and created a legal framework for trade, economic and humanitarian cooperation. Membership in the United Nations since 1992 confirmed the country’s standing as a full-fledged member of the international community.
From the outset, independence was therefore regarded not merely as a political and legal status, but as a practical opportunity to determine the course of national development independently, protect citizens’ interests and build relations with other states on the basis of mutual respect and equality.
Restoring and strengthening statehood required considerable effort. Yet it was during this period that the foundations were laid for Kazakhstan’s modern institutional system, its international standing and its long-term development strategy.
Kazakhstan in a Changing International Order
Since the early years of independence, Kazakhstan has pursued a foreign policy grounded in the protection of national interests, the development of good-neighbourly relations, pragmatism and cooperation with diverse centres of global economic and political influence. The country’s geographic position and international economic ties make a broad range of partnerships and the ability to navigate complex global interdependencies an objective necessity.
In this context, a multi-vector foreign policy means seeking constructive relations with states and international organisations on the basis of sovereign equality, respect for territorial integrity, non-interference in internal affairs and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Its practical value lies in expanding diplomatic room for manoeuvre, economic cooperation and the protection of national interests.
As geopolitical tensions intensify, preserving international law and the effectiveness of multilateral institutions becomes especially important. For states with an interest in stability, predictability and free trade, compliance with international norms is an essential precondition for long-term development.
Kazakhstan consistently supports dialogue and multilateral cooperation within the United Nations. The country’s priorities include international security, sustainable development, nuclear non-proliferation, confidence-building and resolving regional issues through negotiations. These priorities are reflected in the Concept of the Foreign Policy of the Republic of Kazakhstan for 2020–2030.
Nuclear disarmament occupies a special place in Kazakhstan’s international profile. The decision to close the Semipalatinsk Nuclear Test Site in 1991 and the subsequent renunciation of the inherited nuclear arsenal were important milestones in the country’s history and in international security policy. This experience remains a significant part of Kazakhstan’s contribution to global efforts to prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons and strengthen international trust.
The regional dimension of foreign policy is also strategically important. Central Asia’s resilience depends on the development of trade ties, the rational use of water resources, transport connectivity, energy cooperation and joint efforts to address environmental challenges. None of these issues can be effectively resolved by countries acting alone.
Closer cooperation among the countries of Central Asia expands the region’s ability to pursue independent economic development, enhance its international competitiveness and respond to shared challenges in a coordinated manner. Kazakhstan regards regional stability and development as important conditions for its own long-term security and prosperity.
At the same time, the country is interested in deepening engagement with the European Union and its member states. European partners are of considerable interest in industry, energy, transport, education, science, digital technologies and environmental modernisation. For Kazakhstan, such cooperation offers a way to expand export opportunities, attract investment and gain access to advanced technological solutions.
Ultimately, a country’s international role is determined not only by its economic resources or geographic position, but also by its ability to turn these advantages into practical results, sustain dialogue and consistently honour its commitments.
Economic Transformation: From Adaptation to Diversification
Since independence, Kazakhstan’s economy has undergone profound structural change. The country has established its own financial system, national currency, institutions for regulating economic activity and mechanisms for attracting foreign investment. The development of natural resources, industry and infrastructure, together with the expansion of trade ties, has enabled Kazakhstan to strengthen its position in the regional and global economy.
Natural resources remain an important part of the country’s economic potential. Kazakhstan has substantial reserves of hydrocarbons, uranium, non-ferrous and rare metals, as well as significant agricultural capacity. The country’s resource base could underpin new production chains, provided that processing and technological capabilities are developed. According to the World Bank, Kazakhstan has more than 5,000 unexplored deposits of rare and rare-earth metals, with an estimated potential value exceeding US$46 trillion.
However, the long-term resilience of the economy depends not only on using these advantages effectively, but also on broadening the production base, raising labour productivity, developing competitive processing industries and creating new sources of growth.
That is why economic diversification, the development of non-commodity exports and investment in high-value-added sectors are of strategic importance. The aim is a gradual shift from a model in which extractive industries play a substantial role towards a more sophisticated economic structure built on technology, skilled workers, efficient infrastructure and entrepreneurial initiative.
Kazakhstan’s economic performance in recent years reflects both growing business activity and the ongoing challenge of diversification.

The package covers railways, critical minerals, finance and technology, with major US firms involved. Uzbek President Mirziyoyev outlined measures to attract investors, while business executives told Euronews that commercial activity is growing.
Uzbekistan has announced 54 agreements and proposed projects with American partners worth nearly $12bn (€10.7bn), following high-level meetings in Samarkand attended by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Rubio met President Shavkat Mirziyoyev on Monday, with the two discussing trade, energy, critical minerals, aviation and technology. The two countries are seeking to expand their strategic partnership through private investment and joint industrial projects.
According to the Uzbek presidency, bilateral trade has increased by 35% since the beginning of the year, although it did not specify the comparison period.
New priorities for US investment
Senior officials and American business representatives attended the second meeting of the American-Uzbek Business and Investment Council, where the economic agenda was developed.
Mirziyoyev described the council as an important mechanism for developing joint projects, emphasising its distinctive role in Uzbekistan's international economic relations.
"We do not have this kind of format with any other country of the world," he said during his meeting with Rubio.
The Uzbek president announced a package of 54 agreements and prospective initiatives valued at around $12bn and called for a comprehensive action plan to support their implementation.
He also proposed a new approach to attracting investors, under which projects would be prepared with land, infrastructure, permits and administrative requirements already addressed.
Uzbek companies would be encouraged to participate as partners, while a newly established direct investment fund could help finance eligible projects.
Mirziyoyev identified critical minerals, renewable energy, electricity storage, data centres and artificial intelligence as priority areas. He also proposed a joint trade, investment and technology cooperation programme extending to 2035.
The council is co-chaired by Head of Uzbekistan's Presidential Administration Saida Mirziyoyeva and US Special Envoy Sergio Gor.
Mirziyoyeva encouraged US companies to bring investment proposals and practical problems directly to the council, positioning it as a mechanism for resolving obstacles rather than simply discussing future cooperation.
US investors praise growing activity
Business representatives interviewed by Euronews in Samarkand identified opportunities in mining, agriculture and financial services.
Dan Patterson, CEO of Silver Leaf International, pointed to the potential for Uzbek fruit exports to reach US consumers and for US companies to invest in mineral development.
"So there's also tremendous opportunity for minerals and mining advancements in almost every sector," Patterson told Euronews.
Quinn Martin, president of Bluestone, said US investment activity had accelerated after several years of discussions.
"Just my firm has been involved in three transactions in the last five months regarding US investors," he told Euronews.
According to Martin, the transactions involved Uzbekistan's national investment fund, banking and hospitality. He expects US investment to increase further over the coming years.
Uzbekistan's Deputy Minister of Investment, Industry and Trade Shokhrukh Gulyamov also described discussions with US financial institutions.
"Citigroup, one of the leading financial institutions in the United States, is in discussions with our banks about providing financing for various projects," Gulyamov told Euronews.
He also highlighted cooperation with Boeing, including aircraft deliveries and the supply of spare parts needed for maintenance.
Which companies are involved in the agreements?
According to Uzbekistan's Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade, the agreements and proposed initiatives cover transport, energy, critical minerals, finance, digital technologies, agriculture and healthcare.
Railway manufacturer Wabtec is discussing locomotive supplies, maintenance services and local component production.
Financial cooperation involving Franklin Templeton, Oppenheimer & Co, Citigroup and BlackRock includes access to international capital markets, institutional investment and infrastructure financing.
In critical minerals, projects involving ReElement Technologies, Traxys and Trafigura cover geological exploration, processing technologies and mineral supplies.
Other initiatives include satellite communications with Amazon Leo, medical technologies with GE HealthCare and agricultural development with Valmont Industries.

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. Azerbaijan and the countries located along the Middle Corridor provide a stable transport connection between Asia and Europe against the background of ongoing regional conflicts, the Chairman of the Board of the Center for Analysis of International Relations and Multiculturalism (AIR Center), Farid Shafiyev, said at the conference "Middle Corridor and prospects of Eurasian transport connectivity: Azerbaijan and Korea" in Baku on Tuesday, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.
According to Shafiyev, in recent years, the foreign policy of Azerbaijan has strengthened its eastern direction, including within the framework of international platforms and organizations.
"Azerbaijan is looking for various options and alternatives in this complex and complex geopolitical situation. The increase in the flow of goods along the Middle Corridor indicates the growth in demand for this route. The same applies to growing trade.
The country sees good prospects for the development of trade and investment in bilateral relations with the Republic of Korea. Azerbaijan introduced a visa-free regime for citizens of Korea, expressing hope for the development of tourist exchanges between the two countries," he noted.
Shafiyev also highlighted Azerbaijan's participation in international cooperation formats, including the Council on Cooperation and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA), the Organization of Turkic States, the Association of Southeast Asian States (ASEAN) and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization.
The Middle Corridor is a multimodal trade and transport route connecting Asia and Europe through Central Asia, the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Türkiye. The route begins in China and runs through Central Asia before crossing the Caspian Sea and continuing through Azerbaijan, Georgia and Türkiye to European markets.
The Middle Corridor is being developed as an alternative to traditional northern and southern transport routes, providing connectivity between Asian markets, including China, and Europe.
